### The reason for the reprinting

## TO THE KIND

# READER.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'N' containing a floral and foliage pattern.</image-desc>
No sooner had my *Guide to Chemistry* come off the presses—even though it was then an unformed embryo <note>The author uses this biological metaphor to describe the early, incomplete state of his work.</note>—than it made the presses groan in other places <note>original: "fece strider li torchi," an idiomatic way of saying other publishers were busily pirating his work.</note>. This brought me infinite pleasure, seeing that my labors were appreciated by the world; however, it deeply displeased me to see the work wandering through the world <note>original: "l’Orbe," referring to the globe or world.</note> without the escort I had assigned to it of the Most Serene Patron <note>The "escort" refers to the official protection and dedication to Francesco II d'Este, Duke of Modena.</note>. Furthermore, these other publishers criticized the printing of Modena <note>original: "Modona," an archaic spelling of the city.</note> as being less worthy than their own. They believed they were reprinting it more correctly because of some typos <note>original: "lettere false," literally "false letters."</note> that had slipped into that edition, and yet they themselves allowed very gross errors to escape regarding the dosages of the medicines. In place of drams <term>dram: a small pharmaceutical unit of weight (approx. 3.9 grams).</term> they have put ounces <term>ounce: a much larger unit of weight (approx. 28-30 grams). Substituting an ounce for a dram creates a dangerously high dosage.</term>. They also removed the index of notable things and illnesses—a thing so necessary in such a work—wishing to present themselves almost as "Reformers" of my works. Therefore, moved by these reasons, and taking the opportunity to bring the third part to light, I am having the first and second parts reprinted as well.

<summary>Carlo Lancillotti explains that he is reprinting the first two parts of his chemical guide alongside a new third part to correct dangerous dosage errors and omissions found in unauthorized "pirated" editions.</summary>

# TO THE READER.

**S**eeing, oh Friend Reader, the great progress derived from the Most Noble Art of Chemistry <term>Chimica: At this time, chemistry and alchemy were often intertwined, focusing on the purification of substances for medical use</term>, by means of the celebrated remedies that are extracted from mixed bodies <term>Corpi misti: In 17th-century science, these were substances composed of various elements or principles that needed to be separated</term> through it, separating the pure from the impure, that which is incapable of corruption from the corruptible, the medicine from the poison; rendering even the most deleterious and malignant substance—through its preparation—gentle and benign in its effects, and without any danger to the sick, having separated the heterogeneous <term>Heterogeneous: In this context, the unlike or foreign parts that contaminate a substance</term> and impure parts from the homogeneous <term>Homogeneous: The pure, consistent essence of a substance</term> and pure ones. This (as we shall show by proof) cannot be achieved by any other common preparation. Even though some, presenting themselves as true followers of Galen <note>Galen of Pergamon (129–216 AD) was the foundational authority in Roman medicine. His "humoral" theories—based on balancing fluids in the body—often clashed with the "chemical" or "iatrochemical" medicine championed by authors like Lancillotti.</note>, Prince of Medicine, unjustly despise it, seeking every possible way to annihilate it entirely, if their strength were sufficient for such an enterprise. But everything they attempt against it results in nothing but their own confusion, since they prove to be not true and just, but rather false and unjust followers of the aforementioned Galen; whose thought, as is clearly seen through his works, was never anything other than to help his neighbor; who, knowing how

# GUIDE
## TO
### CHEMISTRY
#### *BOOK ONE.*

->*Definition of Chemistry:*<-

->*Chapter One.*<-

It is right, before dealing with this noble **Art**, to provide some explanation so as to know what it is, as well as the **Etymology** <term>Etymology: The study of the origin of words and the way in which their meanings have changed throughout history</term> of its name, its object, and its purpose. To begin, we shall say that **Chemistry** is an **Art** which teaches how to dissolve every **mixed body** <term>Mixed body: In early science, a "mixed body" (corpus mixtum) referred to any substance composed of the four elements—earth, air, fire, and water—combined in specific proportions</term>, and to coagulate it once it has been dissolved. The name of **Chemistry** derives from nothing other than *Chymia*, a Greek name <note>original: "Chimia," likely referring to the Greek χυμεία (khumeia), relating to the pouring or melting of metals</note>, signifying in the common tongue the art of reducing solid things into a **liquid** <note>original: "liquore," referring here to a state of solution or fluidity rather than just an alcoholic beverage</note>, so called because

<summary>This opening page of Book One defines chemistry as the art of dissolving and coagulating matter and begins to explain the Greek etymology of the word "Chemistry."</summary>
<keywords>definition of chemistry, etymology, mixed bodies, coagulation, dissolution, Chymia, Greek origins</keywords>

--- Page 19 ---
<meta>This page continues the definition of chemistry from the previous page, specifically focusing on its various names, its classification as a practical science, and its primary object of study: the mixed body. The catchword from the previous page ("so called because") leads directly into the description of the art's excellence.</meta>

excellence, as it teaches how to dissolve the most solid things, and to coagulate the most liquid. If anyone wishes to call it **Alchemy** <note>original: "Alchimia"</note>, in imitation of the Arabs, this name shall denote its excellence. If called **Spagyrics** <term>Spagyrics: From the Greek words 'spao' (to tear apart) and 'ageiro' (to gather), referring to the process of separating a substance into its components and then recombining them in a purified form</term>, it will demonstrate its most beautiful and primary functions; and if **Hermetic Art**, it will bear witness to its great antiquity <note>referring to the legendary figure Hermes Trismegistus, the purported founder of the alchemical tradition</note>. Since all sciences are either theoretical or practical, and because **Chemistry** is not content with the mere knowledge and contemplation of the **mixed body** <term>Mixed body: Any substance composed of the four elements (earth, air, fire, water) in combination</term>—as **Physics** <note>original: "Fisica," here meaning Natural Philosophy or the study of nature</note> is—but has as its goal operation and manipulation, it therefore deserves its place among the **practical sciences**.

The object of **Chemistry** is the mixed and composite body—not as something "mobile" (which, in this consideration, belongs only to Physics), but as something that is soluble and coagulable. The **mixed body** is either imperfectly or perfectly mixed. It is imperfectly mixed in things such as dew, hail, and snow; it is perfectly mixed in things such as plants, stones, metals, and animals of every species.

The purpose of **Chemistry** is to prepare **medicines** in such a way that they are more pleasing to the taste, more beneficial to the body, and reduced to a smaller quantity, while maintaining their activity and being less harmful in their operations. But someone might say that, although the **Spagyrists** <note>Practitioners of spagyric or chemical medicine</note> boast of the grace and sweetness of their remedies, they nevertheless owe the praise of being more beneficial and safe

The **Chemist** <note>original: "Chimico." In this context, it refers to a practitioner of Spagyry or early alchemy.</note> has therefore chosen fire to fulfill his desire, as the primary among all active qualities, and the most noble among all **sublunary** <note>In the traditional Aristotelian worldview, the "sublunary" sphere is the region of the cosmos below the moon, made of the four elements and subject to change and decay.</note> things, and the cause of every mixture and perfection. And although he sometimes makes use of the Sun, and at other times of **Manure** <note>original: "Letame." Decomposing manure was a common source of gentle, steady heat for alchemical processes like "digestion."</note>, he nevertheless finds that Fire, being more obedient, is most suited to him, as he can more easily increase and diminish it, and also, if it is in a portable place, move it from place to place.

Within Fire, four marvelous effects are observed. The first is that, whereas in any other place all other sublunary bodies, after their generation, subsist and remain for some time, Fire alone has its essence fixed in continuous action, flowing without ceasing like a river.

The second is that it draws from nature the remedy for this continuous flow, finding—through the power it has to spread and multiply—its nourishment within the **mixed body** <note>original: "corpo misto." A substance composed of the four elements, as opposed to a simple, pure element.</note>, and principally within **Vegetables**.

The third is that, while appearing to be a most simple body, it nevertheless requires two kinds of nourishment: one is a certain **oiliness** <note>original: "vntuosità." This refers to the flammable or fatty principle in a substance (often associated with sulfur) that allows it to burn.</note> or thick exhalation, which is always a mixed body; the other is the air that surrounds it; if all...

## *On Furnaces, and How Many Types are Used.*
### *Chapter 3.*

Having spoken of Fire, it will not be out of place to speak of the vessels in which it is kept and made to be obedient to one's pleasure, governing it according to the matter and the operation being performed. These are the **Furnaces**, which are made in various ways according to the materials one wishes to manufacture. One is called a **reverberatory furnace** <note>In a reverberatory furnace, the heat is deflected or "reverberated" off the roof of the chamber onto the material, rather than the material sitting directly in the coals.</note>; in this, the flame that comes from one furnace enters the other where the material to be reverberated is located. However, the fire must be graduated in such a way that the material (if it is a fusible <note>original: "fussibile"—meaning a substance capable of being melted.</note> thing) does not melt. It is called reverberatory fire when a **retort** <term>retort (storta): a glass or ceramic vessel with a long, curved neck used for distilling substances.</term> full of material is enclosed inside a furnace in such a way that, being covered, the fire and flame surround it both from below and from above. There is also the **melting furnace**, which is made with four small doors in the ash-pit <note>original: "cenerario"—the chamber at the bottom of the furnace where ashes are collected and air intake is regulated.</note>; the

and furnaces; I shall begin with the operations in general that are performed by means of her <note>The author continues to personify "Chemistry" as a feminine figure.</note>.

We have already said that **Chemistry** <term>Chemistry: here referring to the spagyric art of separating and recombining substances.</term> has the **mixed body** <note>In the philosophy of the time, a "mixed body" (corpo misto) referred to any substance composed of the four elements—earth, air, fire, and water—which the chemist seeks to refine.</note> as its object, of which she teaches the **solution** and **coagulation**. **Solution** is of two types: **calcination** and **extraction**. **Calcination** <term>Calcination: the process of heating a substance to high temperatures in air to change its physical or chemical state, often reducing it to a powder.</term> is performed either by **corrosion** or by **ignition**. **Corrosion** includes **amalgamation** <term>Amalgamation: the process of mixing a metal (often gold or silver) with mercury.</term>, **precipitation**, **cementation** <term>Cementation: a process where a solid is surrounded by a powdered reagent and heated, often used to refine precious metals.</term>, and **fumigation**. **Ignition** includes **cineration** <note>original: "cinefatione". The process of reducing a substance to ashes (cinders).</note> and **reverberation** <term>Reverberation: a process where heat is reflected or "reverberated" off the roof of a furnace onto the material being heated.</term>, to which is also related the application of **natural moisture**.

**Extraction** is performed either generally or specially. Generally, it is done in three ways: by **ascent**, whether dry or wet. The dry method is called **sublimation** <term>Sublimation: the process of heating a solid until it turns into a gas and then cools back into a solid, used for purification.</term>; the wet method is named **distillation**, which is done in two ways. First, **direct distillation**, which is performed using the **alembic** <term>Alembic: a classic still-head used in distillation to collect and condense vapors.</term> or **condenser**; and second, **oblique distillation**, which is performed by the **retort** <term>Retort: a glass or clay vessel with a long, downward-pointing neck used for distilling substances that require higher heat.</term>. To this are also related **rectification** <note>Refining a liquid by distilling it multiple times to increase its purity.</note> and **cohobation** <note>The process of repeatedly pouring a distilled liquid back onto the solid remains (the "dead head") from which it was drawn to further extract its "virtue."</note>.

**Extraction** is considered generally or specially; generally when it is performed by **descent**, which can be hot—called **distillation by descent**—or cold, which is called **filtration**, **deliquium**, or **failure** <note>original: "defalienza". This refers to "deliquium," where a solid substance absorbs enough moisture from the air to turn into a liquid.</note>. Specially, it is performed by the **separation** of the **tincture** <term>Tincture: in alchemy, the concentrated essential spirit or color of a substance, believed to contain its medicinal or transformative power.</term> from the bodies...

## On Calcination
### Chapter 5

**Calcination** is a reduction of the **mixed body** into lime <note>original: "calce". In this context, "lime" refers to the dry, powdery metallic oxide or residue left after a substance has been heated intensely, not just calcium oxide.</note>, called by **Geber** <note>Abu Musa Jabir ibn Hayyan, a 13th-century Latinized name for a legendary figure in alchemy whose works defined many of these processes for European readers.</note> the "pulverization of the compound." It is performed by fire, such that the word "calcination" derives from the name of "lime," since the calcined thing is deprived of all superfluous and elemental moisture and reduced to a very fine powder. It is done to make substances easier to dissolve. Often, through calcination, the **acrimony** <note>A sharp, stinging, or caustic quality attributed to certain substances.</note>—which consists of a **volatile salt** that is lost through fire—causes sharp medicines to become mild. Others become sharper through calcination, such as **Vitriol** <term>Vitriol: a historical name for sulfate minerals, often used to create acidic solutions.</term> and **Sulfur**, as the watery part that dampened the said acrimony is removed. According to **Geber**, calcination fixes the **spirits** <note>In alchemy, "spirits" were volatile substances that could be easily vaporized or "ascended."</note> of mineral medicines so they may resolve more easily into waters and mix better...

...and furnaces; I will begin with the operations in general, which are performed by means of her <note>The author personifies Chemistry as a feminine art/science.</note>.

**Solution** <note>The process of breaking a substance down into its constituent parts.</note> is of two types: namely, **calcination** and **extraction**. 

**Calcination** is performed either by **corrosion** or by **ignition**. 
*   **Corrosion** <note>Breakdown using acidic or corrosive agents.</note> includes within itself **amalgamation** <term>Amalgamation: the process of combining a metal with mercury.</term>, **precipitation**, **cementation** <term>Cementation: heating a solid in a powder to change its properties.</term>, and **fumigation**.

*   The dry method is called **sublimation**. 
*   The moist method is named **distillation**, which is done in two ways: 
    1.  **Straight**, which is done using the **Alembic** <note>original: "Lambico". A distillation apparatus consisting of a boiling pot and a cooling cap.</note> or the **Refrigeratory** <note>A cooling vessel used to condense vapors.</note>. 
    2.  **Oblique**, which is done using the **Retort** <note>original: "Storta". A glass vessel with a long, downward-pointing neck used for distilling substances that require higher heat.</note>. To this are also related **rectification** <note>Purifying a liquid by re-distilling it.</note> and **cohobation** <note>The repeated distillation of a liquid from its own residue to increase its potency.</note>.

**Extraction** is considered generally or specifically. It is considered generally when it is performed by **descension** <note>Falling downward.</note>, which is either **hot**—and is called distillation by descent—or **cold**, which is called **filtration**, **deliquium** <term>Deliquium: the process where a solid substance absorbs enough atmospheric moisture to become a liquid.</term>, or **desalienza** <note>A rare term likely referring to a specific form of separation or settling.</note>. 

Through an **intermediary** <note>Processes that occur "in between" or over a period of time.</note>, which is done by **digestion** <note>A gentle, prolonged heating similar to the warmth of an animal's stomach.</note>, it is also called **Maceration**, **Putrefaction**, and **Circulation** <note>The continuous distillation and condensation of a liquid in a closed vessel.</note>, to which **fermentation** can be related. 

Specifically, it is done by the separation of the **tincture** <note>The concentrated essence or "soul" of a substance.</note> from the **Bodies**.

## On Calcination
### Chapter 5.

**Calcination** is a reduction of the **Mixed body** into **lime** <note>original: "calce". Here it refers to the powdery or crumbly residue—often an oxide—left after a substance has been subjected to intense heat.</note>, called by **Geber** <note>Geber is the Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, a foundational 8th-century figure in chemistry and alchemy whose works were central to European science.</note> the **pulverization of the compound**, performed by fire. In this way, the word **Calcination** derives from the name for **Lime**, since the thing calcinated is deprived of all superfluous and elemental moisture and reduced to a very fine powder. It is performed to make substances easier to dissolve. Often through calcination, the **acrimony** <note>A sharp, biting, or caustic quality.</note>—which consists of a **volatile salt** that is lost through fire—is removed, causing sharp medicines to become mild. Others become sharper through calcination, such as **Vitriol** <term>Vitriol: a historical term for metallic sulfates, prized for their corrosive and medicinal properties.</term> and **Sulfur**, as the watery part that suppressed said sharpness has been removed. According to **Geber**, calcination **fixes the spirits** <note>To 'fix' a spirit means to transform a volatile, evaporating substance into a stable, solid form that can endure heat.</note> of mineral medicines so they may resolve more easily into liquids, and better mix

In those processes, the bodies of the Metals, through **calcination** <note>calcination: the process of heating a substance to high temperatures in air to remove impurities or change its state</note>, are discharged of their superfluous moisture and rawness, and more easily resolve themselves into spirited waters <note>spirited waters: volatile or alcoholic distillates used in early chemistry</note>. The necessity of calcination is seen in the preparation of **Magisteries** <term>Magistery: a master-preparation where a substance is refined into a concentrated, potent form without losing its physical bulk</term>, where medicines are reduced to an extremely fine powder of great activity without any separation or loss of substance, as is the case with Corals and Pearls.

To calcine or reduce medicines into powder before applying the heat known as **reverberatory fire** <note>reverberatory: a type of furnace or heating method where the flame is deflected from the roof onto the material, providing intense but indirect heat</note> (which, for substances of a delicate nature, must be applied gently and by degrees), they are sometimes quenched or moistened with corrosive liquids. This is done so that, being thus dissolved despite their natural hardness, the fire can better penetrate them. At other times, it is necessary to apply the fire first and then add the corrosives to calcine them; at other times, they are calcined without any additions at all.

### On Corrosion:
### Chapter 69

**Corrosion** is a form of calcination performed on a compound using corrosive substances. It is carried out in several ways, but principally in four: namely, **amalgamation**, **precipitation**, **stratification**, and **fumigation**. These operations are suitable only for Metals.

## *On Amalgamation*
### *Chapter 7.*

Amalgamation is a form of corrosion of Metal, performed with quicksilver <note>original: *argento vivo*; a common historical name for mercury</note>, and it is done when the Metal (excepting iron and copper because their nature does not harmonize <note>original: *simboliza*; referring to alchemical affinity, or the ability of substances to combine</note> in any way with Mercury) is spread into very thin sheets or reduced to filings, and mixed with six or eight parts, more or less, of Mercury. A uniform mass is made of the whole, which, when placed on the fire, the Mercury evaporates and the Metal remains as a fine powder. The use of **Amalgamation** is, in the first place, to purify gold and silver; in the second place, it serves for the precipitation of Gold with Mercury; in the third place, it is used in almost all preparations of Gold and Silver, and in making the Oils of Tin or Lead; furthermore, it serves Goldsmiths for gilding.

## *On Precipitation*

Precipitation is a form of corrosion performed by aqua fortis <term>aqua fortis: literally "strong water," this is the historical name for nitric acid, a powerful solvent used to dissolve metals</term> or other dissolving liquids, according to the diversity of the things one wishes to dissolve. Solvents and aqua fortis <term>aqua fortis: literally "strong water," the historical name for nitric acid</term> dissolve the substance of the Metal, or other things, which eventually settles to the bottom in the form of a Calx <term>calx: a fine powder or oxide remaining after a metal has been corroded or burned</term>. However, to prepare it as a Medicine, a different solvent is required, just as another is needed to prepare it for transmutation <note>transmutation: the alchemical goal of changing base metals into gold or silver</note>.

# On Fumigation Chapter 10.

**Fumigation** is a corrosion of **Metal** performed by smoke or acrid vapor, and it is done in two ways: dry or moist. The dry method is done with minerals—namely **Quicksilver** <term>quicksilver: the historical name for mercury</term> <note>original: *Argento viuo*</note> or **Lead**, or both—to **calcine** <term>calcine: to reduce a metal to a powdered oxide through heat or chemical reaction</term> all the perfect metals by means of them. It is performed in this way: over the molten **Lead** or heated **Quicksilver**, inside a vessel with a narrow mouth, place sheets of **Gold** or silver. These, by receiving the vapor, will become brittle in such a way that they can be crushed and then **calcined** with **Salt**. **Lead** may also [be treated] by means of **Quicksilver** in the following manner: let the **Lead** be melted; then, once it has cooled a little, make a wide hole in it into which the **Quicksilver** shall be thrown. When it is cold, remove it, and repeat this several times until it becomes brittle and can be reduced to powder.

The moist method is performed by putting the liquid or **nitric acid** <term>nitric acid: a highly corrosive acid used in metallurgy to separate gold from silver</term> <note>original: *acqua forte*; literally "strong water"</note> inside a vessel with a narrow neck and placing a sheet of **Metal** inside it, tied with a string so that it does not touch the liquid. Having sealed the mouth very well, it is placed on hot ashes or in **Horse Manure** <note>Horse manure was frequently used by early chemists and alchemists as a source of gentle, consistent heat due to the natural fermentation process</note>, so that the acrid vapors of the [liquid] rise little by little...

## On Ignition.
### Chapter 2.

**Ignition** is a calcination performed by fire, and it is divided into two types: namely, **Cinefaction** and **Reverberation**. **Cinefaction** <term>Cinefaction: the process of reducing a substance to ashes (from the Latin 'cinis' for ash)</term> is an ignition by which vegetable or animal matters are reduced to ash by a violent fire; minerals, properly speaking, are not reduced to ash, but rather into lime. Through this cinefaction, every moisture of the medicine (both essential and accidental) is consumed, leaving nothing more than the salt and a useless earth. 

It is performed in two ways: either open, by means of living flames that incinerate the material from which the **Salt** is drawn; or covered, inside a closed and luted <term>luted: sealed with 'lute,' a clay or paste used to make vessels airtight</term> vessel. By placing it in a **Reverberatory fire** <note>A furnace where the flames are directed or "reverberated" back onto the material being heated</note>, or in a brick or potters' furnace, it is calcined and reduced to ashes, from which the salt is extracted. In this way, the volatile spirits are joined with the dregs <note>original: *Fece*; the solid residue remaining after a process</note> from which the aforementioned **Alkali salt** <term>Alkali salt: salts such as potash or soda ash extracted from the ashes of burnt organic matter</term> is drawn; and because of this retention of spirits, it differs from the first method.

### On Extraction. Chapter 12.

**Extraction** is a type of solution by which the more subtle parts of a **mixed Body** <note>In early chemistry, a "mixed body" refers to a substance composed of various elements or "principles" that need to be separated</note> are separated from the coarser parts. It is of two kinds: one is called general extraction, and the other special. General extraction is performed in three ways: namely by **ascent**, **descent**, and **intermediate means**.
**Ascent** is either dry or moist; the dry is called **sublimation**, and the moist is called **distillation**.
Special Extraction is performed in a way called **separation**.

### On Sublimation. Chapter 13.

**Sublimation** is an extraction of the dry and more subtle parts raised upward by the heat of fire and attached to the top of the vessel; it is performed in this manner:
Take the substance that you wish to sublimate—whether prepared or unprepared, alone or accompanied—place it in the **sublimatory vessel**, and put it on a **sand fire** <note>original: *fuoco di arena*; a sand bath, used to provide uniform, indirect heat to a glass vessel to prevent it from cracking</note> or another heat source appropriate for the vessel and the material. This is because sometimes **earthenware vessels** are used, and other times **glass** ones...

## On Special Extraction.
### Chapter 19.

Special Extraction is that by which the subtlest parts of the mixture (leaving the thicker and earthy part at the bottom) are extracted by a **Menstruum** <term>Menstruo; a solvent used to dissolve or extract the essence of a substance</term> specific to said mixture; then—either by evaporation or distillation of the superfluous moisture—it is reduced to the form of Honey or similar [consistencies], being performed in the following manner. In short, **Extraction** is one of the most principal branches within the **Chemical Art** <term>Arte Chimica; the early modern study of chemistry and alchemy</term>, since by its means spirits, extracts, essences, salts, and other similar things are made.

## On Coagulation.
### Chapter 20.

Having until now discussed **Solution** <term>Solutione; the process of dissolving a solid into a liquid</term> and its types, it remains to speak of **Coagulation**, by which soft and liquid things are made solid by depriving them of their moisture. And although it is almost inseparably joined with the types of Solution—such as **Precipitation**, **Amalgamation**, **Sublimation**, **Distillation**, and the like—nevertheless, it proceeds in a different and particular manner.

First, by **exhalation**, through which the humor <note>The "humor" refers to the fluid or moisture content within the substance.</note> of the coagulable thing evaporates, as is seen in the preparation of Salts. Second, by **decoction** <term>decottione; the process of boiling down a liquid to concentrate its essence</term>, by which liquid things are reduced to a more solid consistency. Third, by **congelation** <term>congelazione; here referring to crystallization or thickening rather than just freezing</term>, as when the crystals of **Vitriol** <term>Vitriolo; a sulfate mineral, often iron or copper sulfate, prized for its reactivity</term>, **Tartar** <term>Tartaro; the crystalline crust formed in wine barrels</term>, and others are made to congeal in underground places, as we will describe later. Fourth, by **fixation** <term>fissatione; an alchemical process that makes a volatile substance stable and resistant to heat</term>, by which volatile things are rendered fixed; though not accustomed to the fire, they become accustomed to it, and this is done either by addi- <note>The text cuts off here, continuing the word "addition" on the next page.</note>

[...fixa]tion of **Fixed Medicines** <term>Medicine fisse; substances rendered stable under heat so that they do not evaporate or fly away</term>, whether by mixture, by **Sublimation** <term>Sublimatione; the process of heating a solid until it becomes a vapor and then collecting it as it solidifies again</term>, by **Cementation** <term>Cemento; a process where a substance is surrounded by powders and heated to change its properties</term>, or in other ways, according to the nature of the thing that one wishes to fix.

## Necessary Rules
# FOR CHEMISTRY
### Chapter Twenty-First

Before beginning to discuss specific operations, having already spoken of the general ones, it will not be out of place—to conclude this Book—to provide some necessary **Rules** to be observed by the practitioners of this **Science** <term>Scienza; here referring to the art of alchemy and chemistry</term>, which are as follows:

#### Rule the First.

That one should have knowledge of the **Matter** <term>Materia; the raw substance or material</term> upon which one intends to work, so that it may be given a degree of **Fire** <term>Fuoco; heat, considered the primary tool of the chemist</term> appropriate to its nature, and that it be placed in a vessel suited to the intended operation.

### Rule the Third

That glass vessels should be tall for subtle and **spirited** <term>spiritose; volatile or highly evaporative</term> substances, so that a single distillation will be more effective than multiple **rectifications** <term>rettificationi; the process of re-distilling a liquid to increase its purity or strength</term>. ### Rule the Fourth

Whatever the distillation may be, take care not to overfill the vessels; for the greatest safety, the **cucurbits** <term>cucurbite; the lower, gourd-shaped part of a still</term> or flasks should not be filled more than a quarter, and the **retorts** <term>storte; a glass vessel with a long, downward-pointing neck</term> up to three-quarters or a little more, and then it must be regulated according to the **matter** <term>materia; the raw material</term> upon which one is working.

### Rule the Fifth

### *Rule the Tenth.*

That distillation by the **retort** <term>Storta; a glass or ceramic vessel with a curved, downward-pointing neck used for distilling substances that require high heat or for dry distillation</term> extracts not only the heavier spirits of minerals, but also the waters and oils of more subtle things, such as woods, roots, seeds, gums, resins, and the like.

### *Rule the Eleventh.*

When distilling **flatulent substances** <note>In early modern chemistry, "flatulent" or "flattuose" referred to substances that tended to foam up, swell, or release sudden, violent bursts of vapor when heated</note>, such as wax, resin, gums, oils, and similar things, one must mix in sand, ash, salt, or other materials, both to suppress their flatulence and to better separate their oily parts.

### *Rule the Twelfth.*

In the distillation of acidic things, such as **vitriol** <term>Vitriolo; a historical name for various sulfate minerals, such as copper or iron sulfate, used to produce sulfuric acid</term>, vinegar, **alum** <note>A chemical compound, usually potassium aluminum sulfate, used as an astringent and in dyeing</note>, and salt, and others, the most ignoble part is the last <note>This likely refers to the "caput mortuum" or the spent dregs remaining in the vessel</note>. Therefore, in **rectifying** <term>Rettificandoli; the process of refining and purifying a liquid through repeated distillation</term> them, one must separate that which distills first and reject it as useless **phlegm** <term>Flemma; the watery, tasteless, and inert part of a substance that lacks the "spirit" or active principle</term>, while preserving the rest.

## *FIRST QUARTER.*

Speaking of the dissolution <term>Solutione; the chemical process of breaking down a substance into liquid</term> and coagulation <term>coagulatione; the process of solidifying or thickening a liquid substance</term> of Vegetables, it will not be out of place to begin first with the Waters and Oils of Flowers, herbs, roots, barks, seeds, gums, and woods, for the first Quarter.

## On the Spirit of Roses. Chapter 2.

It will not be out of place, having spoken of rose water, to speak also of a Spirit that is extracted from them by means of fermentation, which can properly be called "ardent water" <note>original: "acqua ardente"; literally "burning water," a term used for alcohol or spirits</note> of Roses, and it is made in the following way. Take some pink roses <term>Rose incarnate; flesh-colored or pale pink roses, often the Damask variety</term> that have been gathered in clear and serene weather; after shaking the dew from them, they shall be very well crushed. Once crushed, they shall be placed in a glass cucurbit <term>cucurbita; the gourd-shaped base of a still</term>, sealing its mouth very well; then they are put in a cellar or another damp place to ferment. When after a few days they begin to smell sour <note>original: "odorar l'agro"; the acidic scent indicating that the sugars in the petals are converting to alcohol</note> (which must be observed as a sign of true fermentation), one-eighth of the said roses shall be taken and set to distill in the [water] bath <note>the *balneum Mariae*, a gentle heating method using a vessel of hot water</note>. When the distillation is finished, those dregs <term>feci; the spent plant matter or sediment remaining after distillation</term> shall be removed from the glass jar <term>bozza; a rounded glass flask</term>, and another portion of roses shall be put back in, just as before. The water already distilled is poured over them and distilled once more. Removing the dregs as before, the distillate shall be returned again with another part of the aforementioned roses; and doing this until all the fermented roses have been distilled. Finally, all the water extracted from them should be distilled in the bath, separating only the twelfth part—the very first that comes out—which shall be rectified <term>rettificarà; the process of refining a spirit through repeated distillation to increase purity and strength</term> again in the bath. In this way, one will have a most pleasant and fragrant

### *On the Waters of Chicory and other Herbs.*
### *Chapter 3.*

Around the middle of May, take the entire chicory plant, crushing it and cutting it into small pieces. Once dry, they are burned, and from the ashes, the salt <note>In early pharmacy, "salt" refers to the mineral components extracted from plant ash, believed to contain the "body" or salt of the plant's essence</note> shall be extracted using its own [distilled] waters. These will be of wondrous virtue and will keep for a long time.

# On the Waters, Oils, or Essences of Rosemary, Sage, and other similar Herbs.
## Chapter 4.

Take whatever quantity you wish of one of these herbs. Once it has been dried in the shade, place it in the condenser <term>Refrigeratorio; the cooling vessel of the still where vapors turn back to liquid</term> with a sufficient quantity of water, adding a handful of salt. Leave it to macerate <note>maceration is the process of soaking a substance to soften it and extract its chemical components</note> for two or three days. After that time, distill it using a strong fire <note>original: "fuoco gagliardo"</note>, as described at the end of the first Book. Both an Oil and a Water will come forth; after separating the said Oil, the said Water should be rectified <term>rectified; the process of refining or purifying a distilled substance by distilling it again</term> so that it may be used.

The Oils or Essences of Sage and Rosemary are most excellent for all infirmities of the nerves, such as paralysis <note>original: "Parelisia"</note>, apoplexy <note>a historical term for a stroke or sudden loss of consciousness</note>, epilepsy, convulsions, and the like, by taking them orally in a suitable liquid and by anointing the afflicted part.

In the same manner, one makes the Oil of Lavender, Savory, Stoechas <note>original: "Stechade"; likely *Lavandula stoechas*, or French lavender</note>, Thyme, Pennyroyal, and other similar herbs, as well as Juniper berries and others. These must be dried and crushed <note>original: "peste"</note> and distilled just as was described for the herbs.

### On the Waters of Chicory, and other Herbs.
### Chapter 3.

Around the middle of May, take the entire Chicory plant, crushing it, cutting it into small pieces, and placing it in a <term>Refrigeratorio; the cooling vessel or condenser of a still</term>. For every twelve pounds of the said herb, pour over it twenty pounds of common water. After leaving them to macerate <note>maceration is the process of soaking a substance to soften it and extract its medicinal components</note> together for two or three days, set it to <term>distill</term>, extracting no more than eight pounds of water. In this same manner, one makes all the waters of herbs that do not contain much juice, such as Scabious, Mugwort <note>original: "Artemisia"</note>, Wormwood <note>original: "Asintio"</note>, Betony, and other similar plants. 

However, those plants that have plenty of juice within them must be crushed and the juice extracted by pressing; this juice should then be distilled using a <term>bagno; a Bain-marie or water bath</term> or a <term>Refrigeratorio</term>, according to the nature of the substance. To ensure that these waters possess the same virtues and properties as the original plant, one should dry the dregs <note>original: "fec"; the solid remains or 'feces' left after distillation</note> or herbs that remain after distillation. Once dry, they are burned, and from the ashes, one extracts the <term>salt; the mineral essence believed to hold the plant's physical 'body' in Spagyric medicine</term> using its own distilled waters. This process will result in a remedy of wonderful virtue that will be preserved for a long time.

### Figure demonstrating an invention of a vessel for extracting quantities of essence from herbs, flowers, etc., with very little expense.

**A** Furnace where a copper boiler is set in masonry <note>the term "murato" suggests the boiler was built directly into a brick or stone structure to better retain and distribute heat</note>, up to two-thirds of its height.

**D** Bottom of the said small vat, pierced with several holes.

**F** Small barrel filled with water through which the pipes pass.

## Water and Oil of Anise, and Other Similar Seeds
### Chapter 5.

Take four or five pounds of **Anise** <note>original: *Anesi*</note>, and crushing them coarsely in a **marble mortar**, place them in a **cooling vessel** <term>refrigiratorio; the condenser part of the still where vapors are cooled into liquid</term> with fifteen or twenty pounds of common water and two ounces of **burnt tartar** <term>tartaro brucciato; potassium carbonate, used in early chemistry to help break down organic matter and release oils</term>, or two ounces of common salt. Let it **digest** <note>a process of steeping a substance in a liquid with gentle heat to extract its properties</note> in a warm place for one or two days, and then distill it. The water will come out along with the oil, which shall be separated; and in this same way one makes water and oil of **Fennel**, **Cumin**, and other similar seeds, and also that of **Cloves**, which require at least eight days of digestion.

This is the ordinary method as is done in **apothecaries' shops** <term>speciarie; the workshops and storefronts of spice-sellers and pharmacists</term>, which is not to be looked down upon. But wishing to take a little more trouble to make a Water and Oil together of great value, it is done in the following way.

### Of the Spirit and Oil of Turpentine.
#### Chapter 7.

One takes clear **Turpentine** <note>original: *Termentina*; a resin obtained from pine trees</note>, and having heated it, one shall mix in **grit** or **sand** until it is like a paste; then one shall make little balls, putting them into a **retort** <term>storta; a glass vessel with a long, downward-pointing neck used for distilling liquids</term> to distill in the **ashes** <note>an ash bath provided a more even and controlled heat than a direct flame, preventing the glass from shattering</note>, giving it a moderate fire until the **Spirit** has passed through. This Spirit is clear in color, like water; when it begins to change color, one shall change the receiver, and a **yellow oil** will be received. Finally, by increasing the fire, a **red oil** will come out, which shall also be received separately.

The use of the Spirit is very frequent in Medicine, having the following virtues:

First, taken with **Horsetail water** <note>original: *Acqua di Cauda equina*; the plant *Equisetum*, traditionally used for its astringent properties</note>, it heals an old cough.

Second, taken with **milk of sulfur** <term>latte di Solfo; a fine, precipitated sulfur powder used historically for lung and skin ailments</term>, it heals **phthisis** <note>original: *Phthisia*; a historical term for pulmonary tuberculosis or a progressive wasting of the body</note>.

Third, taken with the same, it resists the poison of the **Plague**, being a rare preservative.

Fourth, it drives away all viscosity and foulness of the stomach, taken with **Mint water** or **Wormwood water** <note>original: *Absintio*; *Artemisia absinthium*, a bitter herb used for digestion</note>.

Fifth, it is most excellent for **difficulty of urine** <note>difficulty urinating</note>, and it drives out **stones** and **gravel** <note>original: *Calcoli, e arene*; kidney or bladder stones</note>, taken with **Winter Cherry water** <note>original: *Alchechengi*; *Physalis alkekengi*, also known as Bladder Cherry, used for urinary complaints</note>.

Sixth, taken with **Germander water** <note>original: *Camedrios*; *Teucrium chamaedrys*, an herb used in traditional medicine for gout and internal ulcers</note>, it heals ulcers in the **Bladder**.

It is also made by **descent** <term>a method of "downward" distillation where the source material is heated from above, forcing the oils to melt or vaporize and drip through a filter into a vessel below</term>; that is, by filling a pot that has several holes pierced in its bottom. After sealing the joints very well with **lute** <note>original: *lutando*; "lute" was a paste made of clay, dung, or hair used to make seals airtight and heat-resistant</note>, and also closing the mouth of the containing pot with a well-luted lid, it is placed in a furnace designed for this purpose. A fire is built on top of the pot containing the material for four or six hours, depending on the size of the pot. Allowing everything to cool, it is then lifted gently, and one will see the oil and water in the lower pot, which must be separated and preserved. If one does not have a furnace available, a hole may be dug in the earth, and the receiving pot buried there, along with two finger-widths of the other pot. # ON TINCTURES
## Liquid.
### SECOND QUARTER.

Having spoken of Waters and Oils, to follow the order of progression toward Coagulation <note>in early modern pharmacy, "coagulation" refers to the process of thickening liquids into more solid states like pastes, extracts, or crystals</note>, we shall speak first of liquid tinctures, then of soft ones, coming finally to Extracts, Magisteries <term>Magistery: a refined chemical precipitate believed to contain the essential "mastery" or medicinal soul of a substance</term>, and Salts.

->*On the Tincture of Roses.*<-
->Ch. 10.<-

Place into four pounds of lukewarm water (in which one dram of Oil of Sulfur or Spirit of Vitriol <note>original: *Spirito di Vitriolo*; these are historical terms for sulfuric acid, used here in dilute form to extract color and act as a preservative</note> has been added) one ounce or more of red roses. Leave this infusion in a warm place for three or four hours, and the water will turn red. This liquid should then be filtered, and by dissolving four ounces of Sugar into it, the tincture will be complete.

The aforementioned Tincture is most excellent for burning fevers and other unnatural heats <note>original: *calori preternaturali*; a medical term for pathological heat or inflammation that disrupts the body's natural balance</note>. It refreshes and comforts the liver, aids digestion, and purifies the Blood, taking three or four ounces of it every morning.

# ON SOFT TINCTURES

## THIRD QUARTER.

Soft Tinctures are different from liquid ones because in liquid tinctures—as they do not undergo any coagulation <note>in this context, "coagulation" refers to the thickening or solidifying of a liquid</note>—all of their menstruum <term>Menstruum: a solvent, such as water, alcohol, or vinegar, used to extract the "essence" of a material</term> is preserved. However, in soft tinctures, a portion of the solvent is evaporated away.

## On the Tincture of Saffron.
### Ch. 12.

Take as much Oriental Saffron <note>original: "Zaffarano Orientale"; saffron imported from the East was highly prized in the early modern period for its purity and potency</note> as you wish, and by crushing it, place it to macerate in enough Spirit of Wine <term>Spirit of Wine: high-proof distilled alcohol used as a solvent to extract medicinal properties</term> so that it floats four fingers above it, until the tincture has been very well extracted. Then, add more [spirit] until a whitish earth remains at the bottom; afterwards, the tincture shall be filtered, and the Spirit of Wine separated using a Bain-marie <term>Bain-marie: a water bath used to provide gentle, even heat</term> until it reaches the consistency of honey.

This tincture is excellent for restoring the spirits during syncope <note>syncope is a medical term for fainting or a sudden temporary loss of consciousness</note>, taking only one drop of it within broth or white wine. Furthermore, it is a very great remedy for apoplexy <note>historically, "apoplexy" referred to a stroke or any sudden loss of sensation and movement</note>, particularly if it is prepared with Spirit of Wine in which flowers of lavender and lily of the valley <note>original: "Lilio conuallio"</note> have been previously distilled. It is also an excellent remedy for hysterical passions <note>a historical diagnosis for various physical and emotional symptoms in women, then believed to be caused by disturbances of the womb</note>, and it wonderfully provokes the menses in women.

## *On the Tincture called Oil of Sugar.*

->Ch. 14.<-

Take four ounces of fine crushed sugar and eight ounces of the highest quality Aqua Vitae. Then, place it in a silver or glazed earthenware vessel over hot ashes so that it warms up. Once it is warm, set it on fire with a small piece of paper, and stir it continually with a spatula or a silver spoon until the flame has gone out. Then, add two ounces of Rose Water, mixing it well. The said Tincture is a corroborating <note>a medicine intended to strengthen or "corroborate" the body's systems</note> and most reliable remedy for a cough that proceeds from a cooling of the lungs; it heals difficulty in breathing, coldness, and poor disposition of the chest. The dose is half a spoonful.

# ON EXTRACTS,
# And Magisteries.

## FOURTH QUARTER.

Extracts are nothing other than the juices drawn from dried vegetables and reduced to a solid form, so that pills can be formed from them. In the category of Extracts, one can also include condensed juices, which are different from Decoctions <term>Decoction: the process of boiling plant material in water to extract its medicinal chemicals</term>. This is because in Decoctions, the subtle <note>in early pharmacy, "subtle" refers to the more volatile, refined, or essential components of a substance</note> part of the plant evaporates by means of boiling. However, in the making of an Extract, although evaporation occurs, the essence is preserved because of the gentle heat <note>original: "leggierezza del fuoco," literally the lightness of the fire</note> that must be applied to it.

A Magistery <term>Magistery: from the Latin "magisterium" (mastery); a preparation where the "virtue" of a substance is extracted, dissolved, and then precipitated into a solid powder</term> is nothing other than the virtuous <note>original: "virtual," referring to the "virtue" or the effective medicinal power of the plant</note> part extracted and dissolved by a Solvent <term>Solvent: original: "Menstruo," a term used in alchemy and early chemistry for a liquid that dissolves a solid</term>, which is then coagulated and precipitated to the bottom by some [other] liquid, as we shall describe.

---

### *Of Laudanum, or Nepenthe, called Narcotic extract, that is, anodyne.*

### Extract of Opium. Chapter 23.

Then it shall be filtered, adding new vinegar again as described above and repeating this three times; finally, it shall be evaporated to the consistency of **thick honey**, as has been said.

When these have expired, the vessel shall be opened, separating the essence from the sediment and dregs that will be found at the bottom of it. Keep it in a very well-closed and sealed vessel as a most precious thing, for the healing of an infinite number of ailments, both internal and external.

# Of the Tincture of Salt of Tartar.
## Chapter 35.

Take some <term>Salt of Tartar</term> <note>potassium carbonate, a chemical salt historically derived from the crusty deposits—tartar—found in wine barrels</note> that is very clear and crystallized, and place it in a <term>crucible</term> <note>a heat-resistant container used for melting substances at very high temperatures</note> to melt over a fierce fire until the said Salt has turned a sky-blue color and possesses such a great <term>acrimony</term> <note>a sharp, biting, or caustic quality</note> that, when placed upon the tongue, it burns like fire. Sealing it very tightly, leave it for at least one hour in a cool place; then, place it over the heat for <term>digestion</term> <note>the process of heating a substance gently and steadily to extract its active properties</note>, using an ash-bath or a water-bath, until the said Spirit becomes colored. Once it is colored, the Spirit shall be extracted by distillation, and the Tincture will remain at the bottom of the vessel, red as blood and of a most pleasant scent.

The dose is from five to ten drops in wine, a decoction, or an <term>aperitive</term> <note>a medicinal substance used to "open" the body's internal channels, such as the digestive tract or blood vessels, to clear blockages</note> liquor. # ON VITRIOL, <note>original: "Vitriolo". In the early modern period, vitriol referred to a group of sulfate minerals (such as iron, copper, or zinc sulfate) which were essential in both industry and medicine.</note>
## And its Operations. <term>Operationi</term> [The specific laboratory procedures, such as distillation or calcination, used to prepare a substance for medical use.]
### FIRST QUARTER.
#### Ch. One.

Since Vitriol is the first and primary Mineral that most serves **Medicine**, it would not be right, before coming to the operation, to omit discussing a little of its nature, and we shall say; that among the diverse species of Vitriol we have knowledge of only three, namely white, green, and blue, each of them participating more or less in the nature of **Sulfur**, **Salt**, and **Alum**. Just as the white participates more in the **Aluminous** quality than the other two, and the green more in the **salty** [quality], and the blue more in the **sulfurous** [quality]; nevertheless, each of them is composed of aqueous and terrestrial parts, and between these two, one intermediary [part], which cannot be separated from the other two, except through the intercession of **Mercury**, <note>In alchemy and early chemistry, Mercury was considered one of the three "principles" of matter (alongside Sulfur and Salt), representing fluidity and the metallic essence.</note> which, as **Geber** <note>Geber is the Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, an 8th-century scholar often considered the father of early chemistry. His works were fundamental to European pharmaceutical science.</note> notes, receives that which is of its nature, rejecting that which is not its own. This transparent and intermediary substance,

## On the Spirit of Vitriol
### Chapter 2

Since the **Spirit of Vitriol** <term>Spirit of Vitriol: An early name for sulfuric acid, obtained by distilling green vitriol (iron(II) sulfate)</term> is the first and most principal Spirit among Minerals, just as the **Spirit of Wine** <term>Spirit of Wine: Ethanol or concentrated alcohol</term> is among Vegetables [plants], and that of human Blood is among Animals: it is therefore right to observe very well every necessary requirement in the manner of manufacturing and extracting it; and so, before proceeding, it will be better to declare the way to make a **Furnace** proper for this purpose. This is made according to our custom, without performing great ceremonies <note>The author suggests a practical, utilitarian approach rather than the elaborate, often symbolic furnace designs found in some alchemical texts.</note>, seeking only its quality and that it serves us very well.

Taking one part of potters' earth—and if it is very "fat" <note>In pottery, "fat" clay is highly plastic and sticky, but prone to cracking; it requires tempering with sand.</note> or viscous: another part of Sand or grit; and a little horse dung, *for example* <note>original: "verbi gratia"</note> a quarter part, and kneading everything together very well, let it be reduced to the form of a soft paste. This is to serve as the mortar for building the Furnace. Once this is done, find Bricks that are under-baked <note>original: "mal cotti"; under-baked bricks were preferred as they could better withstand the expansion and contraction of heat without shattering.</note>, and place some of the aforementioned earth where you wish to build the Furnace. Then, place the Bricks in such a way that a small door remains, the width of one Brick, which is to serve as the **ash pit** <term>cenerario: The bottom chamber of a furnace where ashes fall and through which air is drawn to feed the fire</term>. The mouth of the said Furnace should be a perfect square of one span <note>A measurement based on the width of a human hand, roughly 8–9 inches.</note>, and so continue—

## Of the Sulfur of Vitriol.
### Chapter 4.

Take some **German Vitriol** <note>original: "Vitriolo Tedesco," likely green vitriol or iron(II) sulfate, commonly imported from German mining regions</note>; let it be dissolved in distilled rainwater, and by filtering the solution, let it be set to evaporate until a **cuticle** <note>original: "cuticula," a thin film or skin that forms on the surface of a liquid just before crystallization</note> or thin skin forms on top. Once this has formed, let it be removed from the fire and placed in a cool spot to form **crystals**, which shall again be dissolved in similar rainwater. Once dissolved, pour over it **Oil of Tartar** <term>Oil of Tartar: original "Oglio di Tartaro," a liquid solution of potassium carbonate used here as a chemical reagent to trigger precipitation</term> made **by descent** <note>original: "per descenso," a method where a substance is allowed to liquefy by absorbing moisture from the air and dripping into a lower vessel</note>, and you will see the **sulfur of the Vitriol** precipitate to the bottom. Separating this, wash it several times with distilled **cordial waters** <term>cordial waters: original "acque cordiali," medicinal waters intended to invigorate the heart and vital spirits</term>. The said sulfur is a great remedy for those who suffer from **lung disease**.

The dose is from six grains up to one **scruple** <term>scruple: an apothecary unit of weight equal to 20 grains or approximately 1.3 grams</term> in appropriate vehicles.

### Gilla, or Emetic Vitriol:
### Chapter 6.

Dissolve **white vitriol** <term>white vitriol: historically known as "Gilla," this is zinc sulfate, used in early medicine as a powerful emetic to induce vomiting</term> in distilled rainwater, then filter it. Let the said water evaporate over a fire until a film appears on the surface; at that point, place the vessel in a cold place to **crystallize** <term>crystallize: the process of forming solid crystals from a saturated solution as it cools or evaporates</term>. Once the crystals are formed, separate them, and then evaporate the remaining water again until the aforementioned film forms, setting it to **crystallize** as before. Repeat this a third time if necessary. Afterward, take these crystals and dissolve them in **rose water** <term>rose water: water distilled with rose petals, often used in pharmacy to temper harsh minerals or improve the scent and flavor of medicines</term>, letting it evaporate and crystallize just as before. Finally, let the crystals dry in a warm place in the shade.

These crystals gently purge the brain and also strengthen the stomach. They produce marvelous effects in fevers—especially quotidian fevers <note>original: "Quotidiane," fevers that recur every day, traditionally attributed to an excess of phlegm in the stomach</note> that originate from the stomach—when taken with **centaury water** <term>centaury water: a medicinal water distilled from the centaury plant (Centaurium erythraea), known for its bitter properties and use in treating digestive and feverish ailments</term>. They are also excellent against the plague, stomach ailments, catarrhs, and for worms in children.

The dose is from 10 to 20 grains <note>a "grain" was a small unit of weight in the apothecaries' system, approximately 0.06 grams</note> in wine or broth; and for children, 4 or 5 grains are given in a spoonful of **Malvasia** <term>Malvasia: a sweet, aromatic Mediterranean wine often used as a "vehicle" to make bitter medicines more palatable for children</term> or a good white wine.

# OF SULFUR,
## And its operations.

## SECOND QUARTER.

### Chapter Ten.

**Sulfur** is a mineral composed by Nature of the finest part of **Vitriol** <term>vitriol: a sulfate of a metal; in this period, sulfur and vitriol were chemically linked in alchemical theory</term>, so that it is a certain thing that sulfur, before its current existence, was vitriol. It possesses within itself two qualities: one igneous and flammable, and the other vitriolic and non-combustible. The latter, aided by Art <note>meaning "alchemy" or "chemical skill"</note>, reduces the volatile and combustible igneous part to be fixed and incombustible. It is called by some the **Bile of the World**, or better said, of the Earth; by others **Athenian Oil**. To its nature are attributed fatty and oily Mineral substances, such as **Naphtha**, or **Rock Oil** <term>rock oil: an early term for petroleum</term>, **Bitumen**, or **Asphalt**, **Black Amber**, or **Jet**, **White Amber**, or **Succinite**, **Yellow Amber**, or **Karabe** <note>original: "Carabe," from the Arabic word for amber</note>, and the like. Many things are made from Sulfur which serve for Me-

# Of the Spirit, or Oil of Sulfur.
# Chapter II.

The **Spirit of Sulfur**, improperly called **Oil** <note>In this period, highly concentrated acids were called "oils" because of their thick, viscous consistency, even though they are not fats</note>, is made by putting a small pot full of crude sulfur to melt; once it is liquefied, place it under a glass vessel shaped like a bell. Then, by placing a small piece of lighted charcoal inside said Sulfur, it ignites; the smoke that enters the said Vessel will thicken into Spirit, which is collected by placing a small vial at the beak of the said bell. This operation does not succeed well except in humid weather, particularly toward the Equinox <note>the writer suggests that atmospheric moisture helps the sulfurous fumes condense into liquid acid</note>.

This Spirit is nothing other than the Vitriolic part which, as we have said, is contained within the Sulfur; thus, it has nearly the same form and virtue as the **Spirit of Vitriol** <term>spirit of vitriol: sulfuric acid produced from iron or copper sulfates</term>. It is true that, because it is drawn from Sulfur, I am of the opinion—as are many others—that it holds a greater sympathy with the lungs. Thus, it is excellent for obstructions of the lungs, for fevers, **Dropsy** <term>dropsy: an old medical term for edema, or the swelling of soft tissues due to fluid accumulation</term>, retention of urine, and stones.

And externally, it is used for mouth ulcers, pains from decayed teeth, gangrene, and anal fistulas.

# Of the Flowers of Sulfur. Chapter 12.

Since various impurities and foul substances are mixed with Sulfur that can be harmful to health, it must not be taken by mouth in such a state without preparation. For this reason, Chemical Physicians <note>original: *Medici Chimici*</note> have discovered various ways and inventions to prepare it, separating the pure from the impure and extracting its **Flowers** <term>Flowers of Sulfur: a fine, bright yellow powder created when sulfur vapor is cooled quickly and turns directly back into a solid</term>. 

However, as not every kind of sulfur is suitable for this purpose, one should take yellow sulfur in thick sticks <note>original: *cannoni grossi*</note>, as it is the best and most appropriate (just as the green variety is best for the Spirit, as we said above; for all medicinal operations, one must reject that which tends toward a red color, as it is mixed with quantities of **Arsenic** and **Realgar** <term>realgar: a highly toxic arsenic sulfide mineral, known for its orange-red color</term>). 

Then, one shall grind the aforementioned Sulfur and, mixing it with two parts of very clean sand, place it in a pot <note>original: *pignatta*; a deep earthenware cooking or laboratory vessel</note> that can withstand fire. This is to be arranged in the furnace <note>original: *fornello*</note> and bricked in up to the middle, with four holes or registers to be able to increase or decrease the fire. The pot should be no more than a quarter full. Atop this pot, another shall be placed, mouth to mouth and well-luted <note>luted: sealed with a specialized airtight clay or paste to prevent vapors from escaping</note> together. The upper pot shall have its bottom opened, and atop it another shall be placed, which shall be a little smaller than the second, with its mouth fitted to the bottom of the aforementioned pot; and this one likewise with its bottom completely open,

## Balsam and Tincture of Flowers of Sulfur.
### Chapter 13.

Take four ounces of **Flowers of Sulfur** <term>Flowers of Sulfur: a fine, bright yellow powder obtained through the sublimation of natural sulfur, highly valued in early medicine for its purifying properties</term>. Eight ounces of **Oil or Spirit of Turpentine**. The said Flowers shall be added little by little into the said Oil over warm ashes so that they dissolve, stirring continuously with a small stick; once this is done, the vessel containing the Flowers and Oil is placed over a slow fire for eight or ten hours until it has become like pitch. Being in such a state, one shall pour over it enough of the best **Spirit of Wine** <term>Spirit of Wine: high-proof alcohol or ethanol, used here as a solvent to extract the medicinal "essence"</term> so that it floats three or four fingers' depth above it, and it is left to digest with the vessel sealed until the said Spirit is very well colored and red. Then, removing it gently by decanting <note>original: "per inclinatione"; the act of tilting the vessel to pour off the liquid without disturbing the sediment</note>, more [Spirit of Wine] shall be placed over the dregs as before; once that too is colored, all the colored Spirit shall be put into a **Cucurbit** <term>Cucurbit: a gourd-shaped glass vessel used as the lower part of a distillation apparatus</term> in a water bath <note>original: "al bagno"; refers to the "bain-marie" method of gentle heating</note>. The Spirit is then extracted by distillation, and in the bottom will remain the tincture, which may truly be called the true **Balsam for ulcerated lungs**.

The dose is from six up to twenty drops in a pectoral decoction <note>A medicinal tea or broth intended to treat the chest and throat</note>, evening and morning.

## Oil of Amber, Jet, and similar substances.
### Chapter 26.

Amber <note>original: "Carabe"; from the Arabic 'kahraba', commonly referring to yellow amber</note>, although it is held by many to be a type of gum from some tree—and I too was of the same opinion for a long time—nevertheless, some years ago while in France, I clarified for myself through firsthand observation that it is not true that it is a gum. Rather, it is indeed a mineral, and it is found in the depths of the Earth, and does not drip from trees as some believe. This occurred while I was in a place in Provence, France, called Malaugha <note>likely a phonetic spelling of a local village near Brignoles</note>, nine leagues distant from Marseille, six from Toulon, and two from Brignoles. There, I was distilling a great quantity of Jet—called in our vernacular *Zauachio* <note>original: "Zauachio"; an archaic Italian term for jet, a type of lignite used in jewelry and alchemy</note>—extracting oil from it, which I sent to various parts of France, as it was in very great use in those parts for its great medicinal virtue. One day, I went to the mines of the said Jet to collect those pieces which the miners, while digging, threw away as useless for their purpose of making wreaths, Rosaries, Crosses, Pendants, and a thousand other trinkets; these pieces were discarded for being knotty, or having some bit of Marcasite <term>Marcasite: a brittle mineral (iron sulfide) often found in coal or jet deposits; its presence makes the stone difficult to carve or polish</term> mixed into them, or because the Sun had touched them

### Of the Spirit of Salt:
#### Chapter 18.

The Spirit of Salt <term>Spirit of Salt: Historically, this refers to hydrochloric acid, produced by distilling salt with a clay or earth catalyst</term> is a distillation that requires more diligence than other similar ones; and it is necessary to note that Salt, during distillation, requires a graduated and continuous fire that does not diminish at all. For if it diminishes, the distillation ceases, and the business is stalled <note>original: "sbrigato il negotio"; an idiom suggesting the process is prematurely ended or ruined</note>. 

The method, therefore, for extracting it is to take for every pound <term>Pound: a "libra," a historical unit of weight varying by region, but roughly 320–350 grams in early modern Italy</term> of Salt, three pounds of common Bole <term>Bole: a type of earthy, medicinal clay (often reddish) used here as a medium to prevent the salt from melting into a solid mass</term> reduced to the shape or size of Chickpeas—that is, coarsely crushed—and then having removed the fine powder from it. And herein consists the whole **Secret** for being able to extract the Spirit of Salt well and in greater quantity than by pulverizing it finely, as some Authors teach. 

For when the Salt melts, it mixes with the fine powder and forms a solid mass at the bottom of the Retort <term>Retort: a glass or ceramic vessel with a long, downward-pointing neck used for distilling liquids</term>, which then yields the Spirit only with great difficulty. But when it is coarse like this, every piece absorbs the salt separately and, upon being heated to a glow, releases it with greater ease. Ordinarily, from every pound of Salt, at least eight ounces <term>Ounce: an "oncia," 1/12th of a pound</term> or more of Spirit are always extracted, from which the phlegm <term>Phlegm: the watery, inactive part of a distillate that lacks the potency of the "spirit"</term> must be separated. ### Sublimation of Sal Ammoniac
### Chapter 20.

Take eight ounces of Sal Ammoniac <term>Sal Ammoniac: ammonium chloride, a salt used historically in metalworking and medicine</term> and six ounces of iron scales—that which falls off when striking iron upon the anvil—let them be crushed, and mixing them very well, let them be placed in a vessel suitable for this purpose to be sublimated <term>Sublimation: the process of heating a substance until it turns directly from a solid into a vapor and then back to a solid, used here to purify the salt</term> over a strong fire. Once it has been sublimated, let the vessel cool, and by breaking it, the sublimated part shall be separated and mixed with two or three ounces of prepared common salt. Repeat this operation five or six times, always adding new salt; the salt that remains after each sublimation can also be used to extract its Spirit <term>Spirit: in early chemistry, a volatile liquid or essence obtained through distillation</term>.

The aforementioned Sal Ammoniac prepared in this way is an excellent diaphoretic <term>Diaphoretic: a medicinal substance that induces sweating, believed to help the body expel "ill humors" or fevers</term> for every kind of fever, taking twelve or more grains <term>Grain: a historical unit of weight equivalent to about 65 milligrams</term> in appropriate waters <note>In this context, "appropriate waters" refers to specific herbal distillates or infusions intended to carry the medicine.</note>.

### *Of Aqua Fortis. Chapter 23.*

"Luted" means sealed with clay or paste to prevent leaks.</term>, as was said regarding the Spirit.

**Aqua Regia** <term>Aqua Regia: "Regal Water," a mixture of acids capable of dissolving "noble" metals like gold which ordinary Aqua Fortis cannot touch.</term> is made by dissolving three or four ounces of pure **Sal Ammoniac** <term>Sal Ammoniac: Ammonium chloride, a salt that provides the chlorine necessary to turn nitric acid into Aqua Regia.</term> into one pound of Spirit of Niter or Aqua Fortis, and it is distilled using an ash bath <note>A method of heating a vessel evenly by nesting it in a container of hot ashes.</note> in a flask and Retort.

**Aqua de Tribus** <note>literally "Water of the Three."</note>, which serves for various chemical preparations, is made with Saltpeter, Alum (as described above), and Vitriol calcined <note>Vitriol (metal sulfates) "calcined" or heated until it loses its water content and turns yellow.</note> over the fire until it turns yellow, of each an equal part, distilling as above.

# ON ANTIMONY.

## FOURTH SECTION

### Chapter 24.

Antimony is a mineral that comes closer to a metallic nature than any other mineral. It is called by *Basil Valentine* <note>A legendary 15th-century alchemist, likely a pseudonym, whose works popularized the use of antimony in medicine.</note> in his *Triumph of Antimony* the "King of Minerals," and by others—including *Americus Poppius* <note>original: "Ameri Popei" — referring to the German physician Johannes Poppius (16th–17th c.).</note> in his *Basilica of Antimony* <note>original: "Basilica Antimonij"</note>—the *Root of Metals*. By *Quercetanus* <note>Joseph Duchesne (c. 1544–1609), a prominent French physician and advocate for chemical medicine.</note> it is called the *Magnesia of Saturn* <note>In alchemy, "Saturn" often represents lead; Magnesia refers to a primal, magnetic, or essential substance.</note>, along with many other various names and titles. Because it is not my intention to prolong this discourse, I shall omit them. I can well say that through it, when prepared as it should be, the physician shall triumph and achieve victory over every infirmity, no matter how grave or long-standing it may be.

This is also that mineral which, by means of <term>spagyric</term> <note>The alchemical process of separating, purifying, and recombining natural substances to create potent medicines.</note> preparation, can be reduced to one's will and power: now an <term>emetic</term> <note>a substance that induces vomiting</note>, now a <term>cathartic</term> <note>a purgative or laxative</note>, now a <term>diaphoretic</term> <note>a substance that induces sweating</note>, now a <term>diuretic</term> <note>a substance that increases the production of urine</note>, now an <term>alterative</term> <note>a medicine that gradually restores healthy bodily functions</note>, or now a <term>corroborant</term> <note>a tonic or strengthening medicine</note>. Finally, as we shall partly show in this Section through the description of some of the most common remedies, it will be recognized as being more useful in medicine than any other sublunary body <note>The "sublunary" realm refers to everything on Earth beneath the moon, subject to change and decay.</note>.

<summary>This chapter introduces Antimony as the "King of Minerals," highlighting its supreme importance in alchemical medicine and its ability to be transformed into various types of healing treatments.</summary>

# On the Calcination of Antimony, and its
## Flowers. Chapter 25.

Since <term>Calcinated</term> <note>Heated to a high temperature to drive off impurities or change the physical state into a powder.</note> Antimony is necessary for the Extraction of the Tincture and Flowers of Antimony, we shall first describe the method of Calcinating it. This is done in various ways, as we shall explain when describing the different operations; and for the Flowers & Tincture, it is done in the following manner. 

Take a desired quantity of finely ground Antimony and place it in an earthen vessel with a flat bottom, such as an earthen pan. Placing it over a moderate fire and stirring it constantly with a small iron rod until it no longer smokes nor smells of Sulfur, and changes to the color of white ash. If during the said calcination <note>The original Italian manuscript shows a horizontal strike-through on the "zi" in the word "calcinazione".</note> any portion of the said Antimony should melt and form grains, it shall be ground again and returned to Calcination until it is as I have said. Once this is done, let it be set to <term>sublimate</term> <note>A process where a substance is heated into a vapor and then collected as it solidifies again on a cooler surface.</note> in an earthen vessel for the space of twelve or fourteen hours, or more, depending on the quantity there is. 

And let it be given a strong fire, and when the sublimation is finished, the <term>alludels</term> <note>Specialized earthenware pots or condensers used in sublimation, typically stacked on top of each other to catch the vapor as it cools.</note> that are above the vessel containing the Antimony shall be removed; and the <term>Flowers</term> <note>In this context, "Flowers" refers to the pure crystalline powder that has condensed at the top of the vessel after heating.</note> shall be taken, from which the Tincture will be extracted as we shall describe in the following chapter.
