### Most Excellent Tincture of the Flowers of Antimony. Chapter 26.

Have an earthenware vessel made, which should have a narrow mouth and be sufficiently large, with a base shaped almost like an egg; place the Flowers inside, so that they fill no more than a fourth of the vessel. Cover it with a lid made specifically for it, and seal it very well with luting <note>A paste or cement used to make laboratory vessels airtight.</note>; it shall then be placed in a vessel filled with ash, entirely buried, and arranged in the furnace. It shall be given fire for one continuous month. This fire, for the first ten days, should be sufficient to keep the ash warm enough that a hand can be held over it for the duration of a *Hail Mary* <note>original: "Aue Maria"; a common early modern measurement of time based on the prayer's length, approximately 15–20 seconds.</note>. For the next ten days, the ash should be very hot; and for the final ten, it should burn so that in the last three days, if a little sulfur <note>original: "Solfo"</note> is placed on top, it catches fire and burns. Once this time has passed and everything has cooled, the material shall be removed; after crushing it, place it in a glass vessel or flask, and pour distilled vinegar <note>original: "Aceto ſtillato"</note> over it—which should be concentrated <note>The text uses "alcolizato," which in this context refers to a purified or highly rectified vinegar rather than modern alcohol.</note>—so that it floats six or eight fingers deep above it. Place said vessel in a bath to digest <note>A warm bath used for slow chemical extraction.</note> until the vinegar becomes a deep red. This shall be poured off by decanting <note>original: "per inclinatione"; tilting the vessel to pour out the liquid while leaving the solids behind.</note>, adding fresh vinegar on top and repeating the process until the vinegar no longer changes color. Then, put all the vinegar together into a very well-luted <note>The text breaks at "lu-"; the catchword "tata" completes the word "lutata," meaning sealed with clay or wax.</note>

## **Antimonial Febrifuge:** <note>A medicine used to reduce or eliminate fever.</note>
### **Chapter 28.**

Take **Regulus of Antimony** <note>original: "Regolo di Antimonio"; the metallic form of antimony, often purified from its sulfide ore.</note> calcined in the Sun by means of a burning mirror <note>original: "specchio ardente"; a concave mirror used to concentrate sunlight to create high heat for chemical reactions.</note>, and placing it in a flask or vial, pour over it **Spirit of Vitriol** <note>original: "Spirito di Vitriolo"; sulfuric acid, which was historically produced by distilling green vitriol (iron sulfate).</note> so that it floats two fingers <note>A common historical measurement of depth equivalent to the width of two fingers.</note> above it. Putting it in digestion <note>A process of applying gentle, steady heat to a substance in a liquid to extract its active components.</note>, leave it until the said Spirit is thoroughly tinted. This is then removed by decanting <note>original: "per inclinatione"; the act of pouring off the liquid while leaving the sediment undisturbed.</note>, adding more of the Spirit as many times as necessary until it no longer takes on color. Then, it shall be distilled by a <term>water bath <note>original: "per bagno" or "bain-marie"; a method of heating a container by placing it in a larger vessel of boiling water to ensure a gentle, even temperature.</note></term>, extracting the Spirit and the Tincture; there remains at the bottom something like a red and liquid Oil. Over this, **Spirit of Wine** <note>original: "Spirito di Vino"; high-proof distilled alcohol.</note> shall be distilled once, and it will be finished.

The dose is three or four drops in an appropriate liquid for every kind of fever, and it is a most excellent remedy for **pleurisy** <note>original: "pleurisia"; a condition characterized by inflammation of the lining of the lungs.</note>.

## *Wonderful Cathartic of Antimony.*
### Chapter 34.

Take one pound of antimony fused twice, and two pounds of <term>vitriol <note>Metal sulfates, such as iron or copper sulfate.</note></term> calcined until it reaches a red color. ## *Regulus of Antimony. Chapter 35.*

Take 2 pounds of Antimony, and 1 pound each of <term>Tartar <note>Potassium bitartrate, a salty crust found in wine barrels, used here as a flux to help the metal melt.</note></term> and <term>Saltpeter <note>Potassium nitrate, a powerful oxidizing agent.</note></term>. At that point, give it enough heat for <term>fusion <note>The temperature at which the substance fully melts into a liquid.</note></term> for about an hour. Once done, remove the crucible from the fire and, after letting it cool, break it open. Separate the <term>Regulus <note>Original: "Regolo." This can be melted again in a crucible to purify it and cleanse it of all impurities.

## Turpeth Mineral, or a Precipitate excellent above all others. Chapter 41.

Take four ounces of purified Mercury and eight ounces of Oil of Sulfur made by the bell method <note>Original: *Oglio di Solfo fatto per campana*. Sulfuric acid produced by burning sulfur under a glass bell jar.</note>, or Spirit of Vitriol. Place everything in a retort and let it digest <note>The process of applying gentle, consistent heat over a long period.</note> for two days. Then, distill it in a sand bath with a graduated fire, cohobating <note>Original: *cohobando*. An alchemical technique where the distilled liquid is poured back onto the solid remains to be distilled again, concentrating its "virtues."</note> and repeating the same distillation three times. At the end, apply a very intense fire until the retort and the sand glow red-hot. Then, taking the mass that remains at the bottom and crushing it, wash it several times with hot water until the precipitate turns **Yellow**. Over this, burn spirit of wine <note>High-proof alcohol or ethanol.</note> three times, and then it will be prepared.

This preparation of Mercury is an excellent remedy for all infirmities caused by the putrefaction of the humors <note>According to the medical theory of the time, health was governed by the balance of four bodily fluids: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile. ## *Sweet Sublimate, or the "Celestial Eagle" of Quercetanus, or Sweet Mercury. Chapter 43.*

<note>Quercetanus refers to Joseph Duchesne (c. 1544–1609), a prominent physician who advocated for the chemical medicines of Paracelsus. "Sweet Mercury" is known today as calomel.</note>

Take six ounces of purified Mercury. Take eight ounces of the Sublimate made as described above. In a marble mortar, grind and mix them very well until the Sublimate has swallowed all the Mercury, and no grain of "living" <note>Original: *viuo*. Liquid metallic mercury was called "quick" or "living" mercury because of its fluid movement.</note> mercury appears anymore. Afterward, place the mass in a long-necked matrass, filling it only halfway, and it shall be sublimated over a sand bath <term>Fuoco di arena (Sand bath): a pan of sand heated over a fire to provide a steady, even temperature to the glass vessel</term>. The sublimation will be completed in eight or ten hours. Once finished, the vessel is broken and the crystalline part is separated from the raw mercury and the dregs that remain at the bottom, also setting aside the poisonous soot that is found at the neck of the vessel.

*Of Amalgamation. cap. 7* 17 <note>The process of combining mercury with another metal to form an alloy.</note>
*Of Precipitation. cap. 8.* 17
*Of Cementation. cap. 9.* 18 <note>A process involving the heating of two solids in contact with one another—often a metal and a powder—to change the metal's properties.</note>
*Of Fumigation. cap. 10.* 22
*Of Ignition. cap. 11.* 23 <note>Heating a substance until it glows or "ignites" with heat, without necessarily burning it away.</note>
*Of Extraction. cap. 12.* 24
*Of Sublimation. cap. 13.* 24 <note>The process where a solid is heated into a vapor and then condensed back into a solid, used for purification.</note>
*Of Distillation by Ascent. cap. 14* 25 <note>The standard method of distillation where vapors rise up into a "still-head" or "alembic" before cooling.</note>
*Of Distillation by Descent. capit. 14* 28 <note>A method where the heat is applied from above, forcing the vapors or oils to flow downward into a receiver.</note>
*Of the Intermediate Medium. cap. 15.* 29 <note>Original: *Mezo intermezo*. This refers to the substances placed between the fire and the vessel, such as sand, ash, or water baths, to regulate temperature.</note>
*Of Putrefaction. cap. 17.* 31 <note>In alchemy, this refers to a gentle, moist heat (like that of a dunghill or a warm bath) used to break down or "digest" substances over a long period.</note>
*Of Circulation. cap. 18.* 32 <note>A process of continuous distillation in a closed vessel, where the vapor rises, condenses, and falls back into the liquid.</note>
*Of Special Extraction. cap: 19.* 34

# DISCOURSE
## On the Generation of Metals.
### Chapter One.

<image-desc>An ornamental woodcut drop cap for the letter 'H', decorated with floral motifs inside the letter's frame.</image-desc>
Having spoken in the first Book generally about Solution and Coagulation <note>In alchemy, "Solution" refers to turning a solid into a liquid state, while "Coagulation" is the thickening or solidifying of a substance—the two fundamental pillars of laboratory work.</note> in general, in the second about Vegetables <note>In this period, "Vegetables" referred broadly to the entire plant kingdom, not just garden produce.</note>, and in the third about Minerals—all of which we have passed over with brevity—we will now in these pages discuss Metals. We shall seek to expand as much as possible to lead the curious Artisan into the most secret places of this metallic Kingdom. But as Geber <note>Geber is the Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, an 8th-century polymath and a foundational figure in alchemy whose writings heavily influenced European science.</note> notes in the book *On the Investigation of Perfection* <note>original Latin: "de Investigatione perfectionis"</note>, Chapter 2, saying that it is impossible to dissolve a body if one does not know what it is composed of. It does not seem out of place to me to first discuss the manipulations of metals, and then their nature and composition. We shall say, therefore, that in the same way that nature produces plants little by little by means of their seeds upon the face of the earth, similarly—but with a greater length of time—in subterranean places

# ON SATURN,
## and its operations.
### FIRST QUARTER.

<insert>Chapter 2.</insert>

Lead, called **Saturn** by Chemists, is an imperfect Metal of a tender nature, of a dark and pale color, easy to melt, and an enemy to other Metals; its temperament is cold and moist. It is composed of a large quantity of impure Mercury and earthiness, and of few sulfurous parts. But even though it may be the most vile and abject Metal of all others, I nonetheless find that as much utility is drawn from it in Medicine as in Chemistry as from any other Metal. Many kinds of ointments are made from it which include **Ceruse** <note>White lead (lead carbonate), used historically in paints and cosmetics.</note>, **Litharge** of Gold and of Silver <note>Lead oxide (PbO); "of gold" or "of silver" refers to the color or the stage of the refining process rather than the presence of precious metals.</note>, **Minium** <note>Red lead (lead tetroxide), a bright red pigment.</note>, and various other things, which are nothing other than burnt Lead—or to put it better, **calcined** <note>The process of heating a substance to high temperatures in air to achieve decomposition or oxidation, reducing it to a powder.</note> in various ways. But what shall we say then of its **ardent Spirit** <note>Likely referring to a distilled acid or flammable essence derived from lead acetate.</note> and of its **Salt**, since so many different remedies are made from them, as we shall show further on. ### *On the Calcination of Lead, and the method of making Minium. Chapter 3.*

Lead is calcined in various ways, whether with fire or without. This calcination can be called true corrosion, and it is done with the vapor of strong Vinegar, as we demonstrated in the First Book in Chapter 10, page 22; and when calcined in such a way, it is called **Ceruse** <note>White lead (lead carbonate), historically used as a pigment and in cosmetics.</note>. But with fire, it is calcined both with additions and without,

### Spirit of Saturn. Chapter 5.

Take as much **Minium** <note>original: "Minio"; red lead oxide.</note> as you wish, and place it in a glass flask, pouring over it enough distilled vinegar so that it rises four fingers above it—that is, for every three pounds of Minium, use four or more pounds of vinegar. ### *Tincture of Glass of Saturn*
#### *Chapter XI.*

Place the Lead <note>In alchemy, Saturn is the symbolic name for lead</note> inside a wide and shallow Crucible, no higher than three or four fingers—that is, shaped like a Cupel <term>Copella: A shallow, porous bowl used in assaying to separate precious metals from lead; here used to describe the desired shape of the vessel.</term>. Then, place its Muffle <term>Musola: A small clay cover or dome used to protect the contents of a crucible from direct contact with fuel or debris while allowing heat to circulate.</term>, or lid, upon it as one would do with a cupel. Setting it in a furnace with coals all around, blow vehemently by working the Bellows, so that the Lead is converted into a transparent, orange-colored Gum that is fusible <note>Able to be melted</note> and does not evaporate in the fire.

And this is that viscous Mineral Water which, as Rhodianus <note>Likely referring to a pseudo-alchemical authority or a text such as the *Tractatus de tribus verbis*</note> says in his *Treatise of Three Words* <note>original: *Trattato di trè parole*</note>, attracts to itself color, odor, and flavor, preserving the vegetating nature <term>Natura vegetante: The "living" or growth-promoting power alchemists believed existed within minerals, similar to the life-force in plants.</term> of whatever metal you choose. By mixing the Calx <term>Calce: A powder (metal oxide) produced by heating a metal to high temperatures in the presence of air.</term> of the Metal with the aforementioned pulverized gum, and then through the art of smelting, it is reduced into the form of a dark Enamel <term>Smalto: A glassy, fused substance; in this context, it refers to lead glass used to capture the "tincture" of other metals.</term>. By reducing this enamel to powder, it easily communicates its Tincture to distilled Vinegar. Then, by extracting the Menstruum <term>Menstruo: An alchemical solvent used to dissolve or extract the essence of a substance.</term> through evaporation, place the remainder into a Retort <term>Storta: A glass flask with a long, downward-curving neck used for distilling liquids or capturing vapors.</term> to distill. From this will emerge certain cold white fumes, which will be converted into an oil of a vegetating nature.

# Of the Mercury of Saturn. Chapter 12.

Just as there are many curious seekers investigating the **Secrets of Nature** who go searching for the way to make the **Mercury of Saturn** <note>In alchemy, Saturn is the symbolic name for Lead. "Mercury of Saturn" refers to the quest to extract a liquid, metallic essence or "running mercury" from lead.</note>, I did not want to fail in teaching it to them. I will describe it in four ways, which I have extracted from **Schröder** <note>Johann Schröder (1600–1664), a German physician and pharmacologist whose *Pharmacopoeia Medico-Chymica* was a definitive text of the era.</note>, as well as several other recipes mentioned above, which the said Author himself extracted from various authors and brought to light in his **Medico-Chemical Pharmacopoeia** <note>original: *Farmacopea, Medico Chimica*</note>. However, his writings were obscure, abbreviated, and consequently unintelligible to anyone except **Philosophers**, **Chemists**, and those practiced in the said Science. Thus, some who are curious but lack practice "find no juice" <note>A metaphor meaning they find no substance or usable information</note> there. For this reason, I have set it out clearly so that everyone may understand it.

I am certain that I will be blamed by some who are envious of the well-being of others, who will not take it well that I have shown so clearly what so many others have kept secret. If anyone else has described this process, they described it only for the **Sons of Hermes** <term>Figliuoli di Hermete: A traditional term for initiated alchemists, referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of the hermetic arts.</term>. But, considering the liberality of our **Heavenly Father**, who created light as much for the poor as for the rich, and for the good as for the ungrateful, I say—notwithstanding all the detractors who will perhaps be the first to make use of it—that I have desired to make it clear...

through the means of the art <note>In this context, "the art" refers to the art of chemistry or alchemy—the practical manipulation of matter.</note> we see four types of it: namely, that which is called "sweet," which is pure **English Tin** <note>England, particularly Cornwall, was the most famous source of high-quality tin in the Renaissance world.</note>, and this is the kind that must serve us in our chemical operations.

**Lead** consolidates and firms the Tin, and similarly, Tin hardens the Lead. Acting like a **binding viscosity**, it ties the parts of the Tin together. This must be made of a "moist" and a "dry" part, which is the reason why there is no "gluing" of tin with tin alone. This is because from the humidity of the Lead and the dryness of the Tin, a firmer viscosity is generated, which causes such hardness in the mixture of these two metals.

## Oil, or Butter of Jupiter <note>original: "Oglio, ò Butiro di Gioue." In alchemy, "Jupiter" is the traditional name for the metal Tin.</note>

When this is precipitated into common water, it becomes a very white powder; after it has been thoroughly **sweetened** <term>Sweetened: In alchemy, to "dulcify" or sweeten meant washing a substance with water repeatedly until all sharp, corrosive salts were rinsed away.</term> and washed with **cordial waters** <note>Medicinal waters believed to be good for the heart and spirit.</note>, it is a rare **sudorific** <term>Sudorific: A medicine used to induce sweating, which was historically believed to purge the body of diseases or "ill humors."</term>, and it is called **Sudorific Tin**.

The dose is from 4 to 6 or 8 grains with a suitable **vehicle** <note>A liquid carrier, such as wine or broth, used to administer the medicine.</note>.

Both the oil and the silvery flowers serve **Alchemy**.

The aforementioned powder is also a good **cosmetic** for whitening the face, and it is better than **bismuth** or **Spanish White** <note>original: "bianco di Spagna." A common white pigment used in 17th-century makeup, often containing lead or bismuth.</note>.

*It is a certain thing, O friend Reader, that the intention of the Chemist is nothing else—as we have said in the First Book in Chapter one—than to separate the heterogeneous parts from the homogeneous, the impure from the pure. # ON THE PURIFICATION of Mars.

## Chapter One.

<term>Mars</term> <note>original: "Marte." In the language of alchemy, metals were associated with planets; Mars represents Iron because of its strength and its use in creating weapons of war.</note>, or Iron, is purified in two ways: namely, by purging it of its dross (and by gradatory purging) and of its dregs and impurities by winnowing, sifting, and washing it with common water; and by gradatory purging, through which Iron is transformed into Steel, or <term>Chalybs</term> <note>original: "Calibe." An archaic term for steel, named after the Chalybes, an ancient people of the Black Sea region renowned in antiquity for their mastery of iron-working.</note>, and it is done thus.

Take Iron rods, the thickness of a thumb, one part; willow or beech charcoal, ox horn shavings, and chimney soot, one part of each. Let these be stratified <note>To "stratify" means to arrange in alternating layers. This process is a form of "cementation," where iron absorbs carbon from the organic materials to become steel.</note>, first placing the whole in a box of earthenware or Iron made for this purpose, which should have its own lid. First, place a layer of the aforementioned material, then a layer of Iron rods, then the material on top, continuing in this manner until the box is full, and the final layer shall be the material. Then seal it very well and place it in a wind furnace <note>original: "Forno da vento." A furnace designed to pull in a strong draft of air to achieve the intense temperatures required for metallurgy.</note> with a very fierce fire for four or six hours, and it will be done.

It should therefore be noted that <term>Chalybs</term>, or Steel, is nothing other than purified Iron...

## *Reverberatory Calcination, or Astringent Crocus of Mars. Chapter 2:*

Take some <term>iron filings</term> <note>original: "limatura di Marte." In alchemy, Mars is the planetary symbol for Iron.</note>, and sprinkle it several times with <term>urine of a young boy</term> <note>original: "vrina di figliuolo maschio." Historical practitioners believed the urine of prepubescent boys was a pure source of ammonia and salts for chemical reactions.</note> before setting it to reverberate. Then, place a lid over the <term>crucible</term> <note>original: "crociolo," a heat-resistant container.</note> where the said filings are held, in such a way that the lid sits high above the crucible, so that the flame can pass between the crucible and the lid. Then, place it in the <term>reverberatory furnace</term> <note>A furnace that reflects or "reverberates" heat from the roof onto the material, rather than applying a direct flame.</note>, lighting the fire. The <term>Saffron</term> <note>original: "Zaffarano." Also known as "Saffron of Mars," this is a fine red powder (iron oxide) used for its medicinal astringent properties.</note> will rise like a flower within one day; this must be separated every day from the portion that is not yet calcined by passing it through a fine cloth. This removal is done daily so that the powder does not perish from the violence of the fire.

There are also some—and among them <term>Beguin</term> <note>Jean Beguin (c. 1550–1620), a chemist famous for writing one of the first chemistry textbooks.</note>—who take two pounds of <term>iron filings</term> and three pounds of <term>common salt</term>, and putting them in an earthen vessel, reverberate them for twenty-four hours. Then, the mass is taken out, crushed, and washed with <term>common water</term> as many times as necessary until it is sweetened <note>In alchemy, "sweetening" (edulcoration) means washing a substance until all the caustic or salty flavors are gone.</note>. Then, once it is dry, let it be reverberated for eight or ten days until the <term>crocus</term> <note>The red oxide of iron.</note> forms on top. By removing it, one continues to reverberate the rest until it has all been raised into crocus, which must be removed continuously.

### Fusory calcination, or aperitive Crocus of Mars. Chapter 3.

One takes rods or plates of steel and heats them thoroughly in a forge until they are almost at the point of melting. Then, take a <term>magdaleone</term> <note>original: "magdaleone di zolfo in canna." A cylinder or stick of sulfur, often called brimstone.</note> of sulfur and place it upon the hot steel. By the power of the sulfur, the steel will be seen to fall away in granules. These must be caught in a vessel full of vinegar placed underneath. Then, leaving them to dry, they are reduced by pounding into a very fine powder, which may be lightly <term>reverberated</term> <note>original: "riuerberare." To heat a substance in a furnace where the flames are reflected or "reverberated" onto the material rather than touching it directly.</note> for four, six, or more hours until it turns red.

The virtue of this <term>Crocus</term> <note>original: "Croco di Marte." Literally "Saffron of Mars," a term used by early chemists for red iron oxide (rust) due to its color.</note> is to open obstructions, particularly those of the liver and the spleen, and to thin out thick humors. <note>In the medical theory of the time, "humors" were bodily fluids that needed to be kept in balance; "thick humors" were thought to cause sluggishness and disease.</note>

# OF COPPER or Venus, and its Calcination.
## SECOND QUARTER.
### Chapter 18.

Copper, an <term>imperfect metal</term> <note>original: "Metallo imperfetto." In the alchemical tradition, metals like copper, lead, and tin were considered "imperfect" because they were subject to corrosion and change, unlike gold and silver which were "perfect."</note> and a hard one, is also calcined in various ways: either by <term>aqua fortis</term> <note>original: "acque forti." Literally "strong waters," specifically nitric acid.</note>, vinegars, spirits, or by <term>reverberatory fire</term> <note>original: "fuoco di riuerbero." # CONCERNING GOLD,
## And its operations.
### FIRST QUARTER.
#### Chapter One:

Gold, called the **Sun** <term>Sun: In alchemical symbolism, the Sun (Sol) represents Gold, the most perfect and noble of the metals.</term> by **Chemists** <note>original: "Chimici"; in this era, the term referred to both alchemists and pharmacists.</note>, is the most perfect and most noble of all the other metals. It is citrine <note>A deep, yellowish-orange color resembling the citrus fruit.</note> in color, heavy, non-resonant <note>original: "non sonante"; referring to the duller thud gold makes when struck compared to the "ring" of silver or bronze.</note>, shiny, and equally concocted, digested, and thoroughly washed by mineral water within the bowels of the earth. It is created from a most pure fixed substance, from very clear **Quicksilver** <term>Quicksilver: Mercury, believed by alchemists to be the "mother" or feminine principle of all metals.</term>, and from a little pure **sulfur** <term>Sulfur: Considered the "father" or masculine principle, providing color and structure to metals.</term>, containing within itself a fixed and clear redness that has converted the Quicksilver into its own nature. Gold is therefore, among all metals and minerals, of the most balanced and perfect temperament. It is administered in leaves or powdered just so, without other preparation or dissolution; ancient **Physicians** <note>original: "Medici"</note> and modern ones still have made use of it, and continue to use it, to comfort and strengthen our nature, and to drive away from the heart every sad and me-

Then, once more, add the same amount of **Mercury** as the first time and let it dissolve in the same way, until all the **Gold** is seen at the bottom of the **Matrass** in the form of a spongy mass, and the **Mercury** is dissolved into very clear water. This water should be poured off while hot by tilting the vessel <note>original: "per inclinatione." This is the process of decanting—pouring off the liquid while leaving the solid sediment behind.</note>, and the **Gold** shall be washed several times with lukewarm water to remove all saltiness from it. The water impregnated with the **Mercury** can then be reduced into a **Precipitate** <term>Precipitato: A solid substance "thrown down" out of a liquid solution.</term> or into **Sublimate** <term>Solimato: Corrosive sublimate (mercuric chloride), a highly toxic but useful chemical in early modern metallurgy.</term>, according to the will of the **Operator**; in this way, nothing is lost, and you will have a most perfectly purified **Gold** at very little expense.

### . Calcination of Gold . Chapter 3 .

Take the purified Gold, as described above, and amalgamate <note>Amalgamation is the process of alloying a metal (in this case, gold) with mercury to soften it or break it down.</note> it with six ounces of Mercury, reducing the Gold into very minute parts. Then, putting it inside a crucible to heat, likewise have the Mercury heated in another crucible. Removing the Gold from the fire, pour the Mercury over it, stirring with a stick so that they are incorporated together. Then, having thrown it into cold water and washing it very well, let the superfluous Mercury be passed through chamois leather <term>Camozza: Soft, porous leather used here as a fine filter to separate liquid mercury from the solid gold amalgam.</term>, squeezing very well until the mass remains hard. Grind this for a long time inside a mortar of Marble or porphyry with double the weight of decrepitated Salt <term>Sale decrepitato: Common salt (sodium chloride) that has been heated in a crucible until it stops "decrepitating"—the popping and crackling sound caused by the escape of moisture trapped in the crystals.</term>, stirring very well and mixing until the amalgam is no longer visible in any way.

Then, place everything in a crucible, covering it very well with a lid that has a small hole on top. After sealing the joints <note>original: "lutando le gionture." This refers to applying "lute," a fireproof paste, to make the vessel airtight.</note>, let it be heated in a reverberatory furnace for 24 hours, giving it, nevertheless, only such heat that the Gold does not melt. In this way, the Gold will be found calcined <note>Calcination here refers to the process of heating a substance to high temperatures to change its physical or chemical state, specifically turning the metal into a fine, crumbly powder.</note>, and the Mercury, along with a large part of the Salt, will have evaporated and exhaled. Then, take said Gold and wash it several times with water to remove any remaining saltiness; then let it dry. ### Oil of Gold Chapter 5.

Dissolve some Gold in **Aqua Regia** <term>Acqua Regia: "Royal Water," a powerful mixture of nitric and hydrochloric acids capable of dissolving gold.</term>, distilling and **cohobating** <term>coobazione: An alchemical technique where the distilled liquid is poured back onto the solid residue and redistilled to concentrate the substance's "essence."</term> many times using a **water bath** <note>The original "bagno" refers to a *balneum Mariae* or bain-marie, which provides gentle heat.</note>, until an oily substance remains at the bottom of the **cucurbit** <term>cucurbita: A gourd-shaped glass vessel used as the base of a distillation apparatus.</term>. Then, pour over it distilled Vinegar that has been **calcined** <note>Reduced to powder through heat.</note> with its own Salt. Then, withdraw it by distillation and repeat this operation many times, until the Vinegar comes out with the same sharpness <note>original: "acrimonia"</note> it had when it was first added. At that point, all the sharpness that the Gold had acquired by means of the fixed spirits of the Aqua Regia will have been removed. Finally, pour alkalized **Spirit of Wine** <term>Spirito di Vino: High-proof distilled alcohol.</term> over it, and let it digest in a lukewarm bath for a period of fifteen days. Once these have passed, the said Spirit shall be distilled, extracting it through the same bath, and the **Oil of Gold** will remain at the bottom.

### Tartarized Spirit of Wine. Chapter 8.

### Tincture of Gold. Chapter 9.

The true Tincture of Gold is nothing other than its **sulfur** <note>In alchemy, "sulfur" refers to one of the three prime principles (along with mercury and salt), representing the active, combustible, and coloring soul of a metal.</note> extracted from the gold itself, which must remain entirely white; many authors demonstrate the way to extract it, but in such a manner that the method is known to few. However, I did not wish to omit teaching such a great secret for the benefit of those devoted to this art, and it is done as follows.

Taking one ounce of the purest **gold** and six ounces of **mercury** <term>mercurio: Quicksilver, used here to create an amalgam with the gold to make it workable.</term>, then pass the excess mercury through a **chamois skin** <note>original: "pelle di camozza"; used as a filter to squeeze out liquid mercury, leaving a paste-like gold-mercury amalgam behind.</note>, and let the remainder evaporate over a slow fire (having first mixed and weighed it with **common salt** <note>sodium chloride</note>). Then, washing the said mixture several times with hot water, let it dry; and once dry, grind it finely with three ounces of **cinnabar** <term>cinabrio: Mercury sulfide, a bright red mineral used here to "open" the gold or impart color.</term>. Then, putting it into a flat and low **crucible** <term>crociolo: A heat-resistant ceramic vessel.</term> made in the manner of a **cupel** <term>copella: A shallow, porous refining dish.</term>, place upon said crucible a lid pierced with several holes, and let it be set to **cement** <note>original: "cimentar"; a process of heating a metal in contact with other reactive substances to change its properties.</note> in a furnace, applying fire below and above until the cinnabar has evaporated. Then, return the said gold with new cinnabar as before, repeating the operation 5 or 6 times, until the gold remains at the bottom of the crucible like a very red sponge. This shall be ground with 8 parts of **sal ammoniac** <term>sale armoniaco: Ammonium chloride, a volatile salt used to assist in the "lifting" or sublimation of other substances.</term>, **sublimating** <note>The process where a substance is heated until it turns to vapor and then collects again as a solid at the top of the vessel.</note> several times until the golden color is seen to rise; then washing it several times until all saltiness is removed, then let it dry, and the tincture shall be extracted.

### *Potable Gold, or Essence of Gold, Secret of the Philosophers. Chapter 11.*

Take purified gold, as we have previously taught, and reduce it into very thin sheets. Then, having also some **lead** <note>original: "Piombo"</note> reduced into sheets a little thicker than those of the gold, and arranging them in a wide **crucible** <term>crociolo: A ceramic or metal container used for melting materials at very high temperatures.</term>, placing them layer upon layer, let them be **cemented** <note>A process of heating solids in a sealed container; original: "cimentano"</note> for twenty-four hours. Then, grinding the gold and reducing it to an impalpable powder, let it be washed. Once thus purified and dried, pour over it (having placed it in a **matrass** <term>matraccio: A glass flask with a round body and a long neck used for digestion and distillation.</term>) enough **Spirit of Wine** <note>High-proof alcohol; original: "Spirito di Vino"</note> so that it floats six finger-breadths above it. After plugging it very well and sealing the mouth of the vessel **hermetically** <note>A perfectly airtight seal, often made by melting the glass of the neck shut.</note>, let it be placed in a hot bath for digestion for the space of one month. 

At that time, pour out the tinted Spirit, leaving an extremely white powder at the bottom of the matrass, which shall be preserved for the use we will describe in its proper place. Placing the liquid in a **flask** <term>bozza: A glass distillation vessel.</term> in the bath, let it be distilled until it reaches the consistency of an **oil**. This oil shall then be placed in a **retort** <term>storta: A glass vessel with a long, downward-curving neck used for distilling substances at higher heats.</term> and distilled through a **sand bath** <note>original: "per arena"</note>, repeating this four or five times. You will then have an **Essence of Gold** made without any corrosive <note>The author emphasizes this is made without harsh acids like aqua regia, which was a point of pride for many alchemists.</note>, which possesses innumerable virtues.

The dose is three or four grains <note>A grain was a small unit of weight, roughly 65 milligrams.</note>.

# ON SILVER:

## SECOND QUARTER,

### Chap. 17.

Silver, called **Moon** <note>original: *Luna*; in alchemical tradition, metals were associated with celestial bodies, and silver was linked to the Moon due to its white, reflective luster</note> by Chemists, is a noble Body, but not as much so as Gold; it is found alone in specific Mines, and some is mixed with other Metals, and that [mixed type] is not so pure and has need of purification. Silver is generated from a pure Mercury and a white, non-combustible sulfur <note>Early modern chemistry followed the "Mercury-Sulfur theory," which suggested all metals were made of these two principles in varying degrees of purity</note>, and is of a white color, pure and clean, with a ringing tone, durable during **cupellation** <term>Copella: a refining process where ores are heated to high temperatures to separate noble metals from base metals</term>, malleable under the hammer, and it melts with greater ease than do Copper and Iron. Similarly, various operations and Medicines are made from it, but before putting it to use, it must be purified. The method is by means of **Lead**, that is, taking one part of Silver and four parts of Lead, which shall be melted inside a **crucible** <note>A ceramic or metal container used for melting substances at very high temperatures</note>; and when the said Lead is boiling, the Silver shall be thrown into it and melted, applying a vigorous fire until the Lead rises above the Silver like foam, which is **litharge** <term>Litargirio: a mineral form of lead oxide produced during the refining of silver</term>, and by separating this foam, the Silver will remain, purified from every other metal. It is also purified by cupellation, as we have taught— <note>The text cuts off here, continuing the instructions on the next page; the catchword "fegna-" suggests the next word is "segnatamente" or a similar term meaning "specifically" or "notedly"</note>

These two **Vitriols** <note>in early chemistry, "vitriol" referred to various crystalline metallic salts, such as sulfates or chlorides</note> joined together in due proportion and **decocted** <term>decotti: boiled or heated to concentrate a substance and extract its medicinal properties</term> in the **Athanor** <term>Attanor: a specialized furnace designed to provide a constant, uniform heat for long-term "digestion" or maturation of a chemical substance</term>, until they have passed through all the **colors** <note>a reference to the "stages of the work": alchemists believed the substance had to turn black, then white, then yellow, before finally reaching a stable "redness" which indicated ultimate potency</note> and have come to rest in redness; a medicine is made from them that is no less in virtue than the **great secret of the Philosophers** <note>this refers to the *Magnum Opus* or "Great Work," the creation of the Philosopher's Stone, which was believed to grant health and longevity</note>.

The dose is one **grain** <note>original: *grano*; a very small measurement of weight roughly equivalent to 0.06 grams</note> for every incurable and desperate infirmity.

### A Lamp-Furnace Equipped
### with its Vessels.

**A** Copper vessel, which is filled with water, or other [liquid] <note>This likely refers to a water bath, or *bain-marie*, used to ensure the flask is heated evenly and never exceeds the boiling point of water</note>.

**B** **Cucurbit** <term>Cucurbita: a gourd-shaped glass or ceramic vessel used as the boiling flask in a distillation setup</term> containing the material to be distilled.

**C** Opening where the lamp is placed: and then it is closed.

**D** Lamp with three, or four **wicks** <note>original: *lucigni*; multiple wicks allowed the chemist to precisely control the heat by lighting one or all of them</note>.

**E** Holes through which the water enters and exits.

**F** **Flues** <note>original: *Canalli*; small pipes or vents designed to lead smoke and exhaust away from the flame</note> through which the smoke exits.

**G** Small cord attached to the knob of the **cap** <term>capello: the alembic head or "still-head" that fits over the cucurbit to collect vapors</term> to support the **receiver**.

**H** **Receiver** <term>Recipiente: the vessel placed at the end of the distillation apparatus to collect the condensed liquid</term>.

### *Lunar Bezoar: Chapter 21.*

Dissolve the silver with the **Spirit of Nitre** <term>Spirit of Nitre: nitric acid, a powerful corrosive used by alchemists to dissolve metals</term>, as was said in the previous chapter, so that it is well-increased in weight and reduced to a viscous water by means of digestion. Over one ounce of this water, pour ten ounces of well-rectified **Butter of Antimony** <term>Butter of Antimony: antimony trichloride, a chemical compound that has a thick, oily consistency</term>. Then, over this mixture, distill the Spirit of Nitre three times, applying a strong fire at the end of each distillation. Once this is done, let the said material be heated to a red glow for two short hours in a **crucible** <note>a ceramic or metal container capable of withstanding the very high temperatures needed to melt or calcine minerals</note>. After the material has been reduced to powder, burn rectified **Spirit of Wine** <note>original: *Spirito di Vino rettificato*; high-proof alcohol or ethanol</note> over it.

The dose is from six to eight grains for infirmities of the **Brain** <note>original: *Ceruello*</note>, and it is a specific remedy for the ailments of women.

---

### *Mercury of the Moon: Chapter 22.*

Take fine silver reduced into very thin sheets and cut them into small pieces. Dissolve them in **Aqua Fortis** <term>Aqua Fortis: "Strong Water," a historical name for nitric acid</term>, then remove the water by distillation. Afterward, pour more [water] over the said silver four times, always repeating the said waters by distillation. Finally, **cohobate** <term>Cohobation: the process of pouring a distilled liquid back onto the solid residue from which it was drawn to further refine or extract its properties</term> them over the said Moon <note>original: *Luna*; the alchemical name for silver</note> once or twice, all of them together; place the said—

## On the Generation of Man.
### Chapter I.

Now, since Man is the most perfect among all other animals, it is no wonder if nature has employed greater industry <note>In this context, "industry" refers to skillful design or careful, purposeful workmanship.</note> in his generation than in that of any other animal, seeing as three specific things are required for his generation: namely, agent, time, and place. And it should be known that a woman cannot (as some have thought) become pregnant by a single seed—that is, by her own alone or by that of a man—but of necessity it is required that both should intervene. This seed is formed from the purest blood of the man and from all his members; this is clearly seen because if a parent suffers from some infirmity in a specific limb or organ, the children born of them will for the most part suffer similar infirmities. These are called hereditary diseases <note>original Latin: "morbi hereditarij."</note> by physicians; and as they proceed from the radical moisture <term>Radical moisture (humido radicale): In early modern medicine, this was believed to be a fundamental bodily fluid that acted as the "fuel" for the body's vital heat; its depletion was associated with aging and death.</term>, they are extremely difficult to cure—I would even venture to say almost incurable—because they derive from the seed of their fathers.

# On the Humors Most Fit for Generation, and
## other particulars regarding this.
### Chapter 2.

Since we are to speak of generation, it will not be out of place to examine a little which men are most fit for procreation, and other particulars. I will say, therefore, according to the opinion of various philosophers, that among all the temperaments <term>Temperament (temperamento): In traditional medicine, this refers to the specific balance of the four qualities—hot, cold, moist, and dry—which determined a person’s health and character.</term>, those who are of a hot and moist temperament <note>This combination corresponds to the "Sanguine" temperament, traditionally viewed as the most fertile and healthy.</note> are more powerful in generation than those of any other temperament. For instance, those of a hot and dry temperament remain weaker because of the dryness, just as the cold and moist are weakened by coldness; for a temperate heat is required for the generation of a perfect seed.

That the man’s seed is hot is shown by the pleasure a man receives in the scattering of it; for when it has reached the genitals, the spirit <note>In early physiology, "spirits" (spiriti) were subtle, vapor-like substances that moved through the nerves and vessels to facilitate bodily functions and sensations.</note> immediately sends out the seed through the passage, which, being fibrous <note>original: "neruoso." In this period, "nervous" often meant "full of sinews or fibers" as well as being sensitive.</note> and warming itself by means of the said seed, causes delight. It is further shown by the double pleasure that the woman receives in such an act: the first is when she scatters her own seed, and the second when she receives that of the man. Because his seed is hot and enters the womb <term>Womb (matrice): From the Latin "matrix," used in historical texts to describe the uterus as the "place of origin" or "mother" organ.</term>, which is cold, it causes a second delight; and without this, the woman could not conceive. For this reason, one should not marvel—

...[to know] why public prostitutes <note>original: "publiche meretrici"</note> rarely become pregnant: it is because, joining with a man only for pure profit, they take no pleasure. Even if they do take some pleasure and release their own seed, they cannot become pregnant due to continuous use, as they have slippery wombs <term>Womb (matrice): In the medical language of the time, the uterus was often referred to as the "matrix," the vessel where life is formed and "matured."</term> that are covered, and their cells <note>This refers to the medieval "seven-cell theory" of the uterus, which suggested the womb was divided into distinct compartments.</note> are "blind" or blocked, which ought to receive and retain the man’s sperm.

There are also many virtuous women who love their husbands with a most perfect love and yet cannot conceive. This happens either because the womb is very thick, and due to this thickness, it closes the mouth of the womb during the act, thus preventing the sperm from entering; or because, being too dilated, they cannot retain it. Such a defect also sometimes proceeds from the men; for if their sperm is too hot, it burns; if it is too cold, it freezes; if it is too moist, it is slippery; and if it is dry, it becomes hard and cannot be "cooked" <note>original: "concuocere." This refers to "coction," the physiological process where bodily heat transforms raw matter into a perfected substance like blood or seed.</note>.

Regarding the generation of a male or a female, many maintain that it proceeds from the position the seed takes within the womb. They say that when the seed settles in the left side, a female is generated; but when it settles in the right side—which is hotter because of the liver <note>In Galenic anatomy, the liver (located on the right) was considered the source of natural heat; therefore, the right side of the womb was thought to be warmer and more conducive to forming "hotter" male children.</note> located there—a male is generated. But for my part, I adhere to, and find more foundation in, the opinion of those who maintain that if the man’s seed overpowers that of the woman, then a male is generated, and so to the [opposite]—

->*The form and industry used by nature in the generation of man.*<-

->Chapter 3.<-

Once the woman has conceived, immediately from the seed gathered in the womb <term>Womb (matrice): also called the matrix, the organ where life is formed and "matured."</term>, three vesicles <term>Vesicles (ampolle): small, bubble-like structures believed to be the foundations of the vital organs.</term> are formed at the same time. These are the origins of the three principal members: the heart, the liver, and the brain. According to the anatomists, these arrive at perfection in seven days—first the heart, then the liver, and finally the brain. Within the space of these days, the parts from which the bones must form appear clearer and more solid, while those of the arteries, veins, nerves, and cartilage appear thinner and more liquid. This is discerned more openly on the fifteenth day. Thus, the innate heat <term>Innate heat (nativo calore): the vital energy or "fire" believed to drive growth, digestion, and the development of life.</term> found within the seed guides the principal members to their proper places and gives them their completion and suitable shape. Then, the veins are seen emerging from the liver, the nerves from the brain, and the arteries from the heart. ### Of the many varieties seen among men, and their causes, and other signs. Chapter 5.

Among the notable things concerning man, one of the most marvelous is to see that, among such a vast number of people, there is no one who is entirely equal in form to another, even though they may be **twin brothers**, born and generated from the same seed, and having come into the light at almost the same moment. ### *Of the Hair. Chapter 6.*

### *Simple hair liquor to make them grow and increase, and then to retain them if they fall out. Chapter 7.*

Take as much hair as you wish, and cutting it into very small pieces, place it in a <term>retort</term> <note>original: *storta*. A glass vessel with a long, downward-pointing neck used for distilling liquids by heating them.</note> to distill over a <term>sand bath</term> <note>original: *fuoco di arena, ò di sabbia*. A method of heating a vessel evenly by nesting it in a container of sand, which is then heated.</note>; the heat should be applied in stages. With the resulting liquor, one should rub the affected area, and hair will grow matching the type that was distilled. That which remains in the retort should be <term>calcined</term> <note>reduced to white ash through high heat</note> until it reaches whiteness; mix this with <term>styptic wine</term> <note>original: *vino stiptico*. A wine with astringent properties used in early medicine to contract tissues and stop the flow of bodily fluids.</note> in the form of a liniment. By anointing the roots of the hair with this mixture, it will restrain them from falling out.

### *Compound liquor and oil of hair for the said effect, which also makes blond hair grow. Chapter 8.*

Take blond hair, <term>wine tartar</term> <note>original: *tartaro di vino*. A salty crust that forms in wine barrels (potassium bitartrate), frequently used in alchemical preparations.</note>, and <term>citrine honey</term> <note>original: *miele citrina*. A pale, lemon-colored honey.</note> in <term>equal parts</term> <note>original: *ana*. A medical abbreviation from the Greek 'ana', meaning 'of each'.</note>; grind the hair and also reduce the tartar to a powder. ## Water, and Oil of Human Blood.
->Cap. 21.<-

Take human blood from healthy young people, drawn in the Spring at the end of April, or the beginning of May, 24 pounds <term>lir.</term><note>The original abbreviation "lir." refers to the *libra* or pound, a common unit of weight in early pharmacy.</note>. M.</term><note>Original: Balneum Mariae, or "Bain-Marie."</note> and the oil over ashes in a retort <term>storta</term>—it will lose all its stench.

## Wonderful Oil of Human Blood.
->Cap. 22.<-

Take the blood of healthy young people, specifically from those who undergo purging <note>Seasonal bloodletting or "purging" was a common medical practice in the spring to balance the body's humors.</note> in the month of May, and you shall fill a flask <term>bozza</term> or a urinal-shaped vessel to the fourth part; then, by placing its blind head <term>capello cieco</term><note>A "blind head" is a still-head without a spout or "beak," used to keep vapors inside the vessel for circulation or digestion rather than letting them flow out.</note> upon it, let it be placed in the moderate heat of a water bath, so that the said blood, thinning and becoming spongy, fills the entire flask. Take care, however, to proceed cautiously in said distillation, so that the fire is not too strong and does not burn the dregs <note>The sediment or "feces" remaining at the bottom.</note>.

The dose is from two up to six drops in some appropriate liquor <note>In this period, "liquor" simply meant any liquid carrier, such as wine or herbal water.</note>.

### A Very Inexpensive Bath, in Which One Can Distill and Digest Many Vessels at Once.

**A** A furnace in which is built a copper or iron flask, the neck of which enters tightly into a large wooden vessel; this vessel has a lid with several holes through which one places the urinals <note>In historical laboratory practice, an "urinal" refers to a specific shape of glass flask with a wide body and a long neck, so named because it resembled vessels used for medical uroscopy.</note> or vessels, which are attached with small cords connected to the said wooden lid, as is done in other baths.

**B** The Copper or Iron Flask.

**C** A wooden vessel that is filled with water; as the water enters the flask positioned inside the furnace, it heats up and causes the water in the aforementioned wooden vessel to boil.

**D** Various flasks <term>bozze</term><note>original: "bozze"; these were typically rounded glass bottles or flasks used in chemical operations.</note> that are inside the bath for digestion <note>Digestion is an alchemical process where a substance is subjected to gentle, consistent heat over a long period, intended to "mature" or "ripen" the material.</note>.

**E** A bench <term>scano</term> or stand that supports the bath vessel.

# ON THE DEAD PARTS
# Of Man.

## THIRD SECTION.

Since we have spoken of the living parts of man, and the most common operations performed on them, it will not be inappropriate to speak of the dead parts, and thus we will begin with the whole cadaver of man, then follow with its parts individually. Mummy <note>In early modern medicine, "Mummy" (mumia) was a highly valued drug. It was not always an entire embalmed body, but often the resins and fluids extracted from them, or even bodies naturally preserved by desert sands.</note>, then, being the cadavers of men—some of them embalmed, others who died in the mountains of Gilboa <note>original: "Gelboe"; referring to Mount Gilboa. Historical texts often cited this location as a source for naturally desiccated bodies.</note>, or in the Sea of Sand <note>A common historical term for the great deserts of the Middle East, such as the Sahara or the Arabian Desert.</note> having remained suffocated there by windstorms—and others as will be more distinctly declared in this following chapter.

Pour over them the Spirit preserved from before <note>Referring to the mixture of Spirit of Vitriol, gold, silver, and antimony prepared on page 91</note> and let it **digest** for several days. Then, using a naked flame <note>Direct heat from a fire rather than a gentle sand or water bath</note>, all the Spirit shall be extracted in the same manner that one extracts **Spirit of Vitriol**. Once this is done, break the retort, collect the dregs <note>original: "feci"; the solid residue left after distillation</note>, and <term>calcine</term> them by **reverberation** <note>Heating in a furnace where the flame is reflected or "reverberated" down onto the material</note> for five or six hours. 

Then, boil them in **Peony** and **Lavender water** and extract the **Salt** <note>In alchemy, the "Salt" is the purified mineral essence extracted from the ashes of a substance</note>. This Salt should be placed into the aforementioned Spirit, which shall be put into digestion until the Salt is dissolved, and it will be complete.

This most excellent **Secret** <note>original: "Arcano"; a term for a powerful, hidden chemical remedy</note>, besides infallibly curing **epilepsy**, is a unique remedy for **apoplexy**, **paralysis**, **spasms**, **gout**, **leprosy**, and **fevers** of every kind. Finally, if taken in suitable liquids after the body has been purged, it heals any stubborn infirmity. For epileptics, it should be used for one continuous month, beginning during the waning of the Moon...

# *Spirit of Vitriol by Quercetanus, called Anti-epileptic. Chapter 39.*

Take some **Hungarian Vitriol** <note>original: "Vitriolo vngarico"; a high-quality mineral sulfate, often copper or iron-based, highly prized by alchemists for its purity</note>, and having placed it in a glazed earthenware vessel, the <term>phlegm</term> <note>the watery, tasteless part of a distillate that lacks medicinal "virtue"</note> is extracted over a slow fire. Then, it is <term>cohobated</term> <note>a process where the distilled liquid is poured back onto the solid residue and redistilled to concentrate the spirit</note> as many times as necessary until the dry matter absorbs the moisture. Once this is done, let the said **Vitriol** be soaked in the most perfect **Spirit of Wine** <note>high-proof distilled alcohol</note> and let it digest for one or two days in a well-sealed vessel. Afterward, let it be distilled through a <term>retort</term> <note>original: "storta"; a glass or ceramic vessel with a long, downward-pointing neck used for distilling volatile substances</note> over an open flame until all the Spirits have come out. From the distilled liquor, by means of a **circulation** <note>a process of continuous distillation and condensation in a closed vessel, intended to "exalt" or refine the substance</note> of eight or ten days, every bit of dregs and <term>hypostasis</term> <note>sediment or deposits found in liquids</note> should be separated. Afterward, adding to it a fourth part of the weight of the said Spirit of **Crollius’s camphorated theriacal spirit** <note>original: "Spirito teriacale canforato del Crolio"; a complex medicinal preparation by Oswald Croll, combining the "cure-all" theriac with camphor</note>, let it be distilled again two or three times. It serves for the **Extract of Skull** as mentioned above, and it is excellent for **epilepsy**.

The dose is from 4 up to 12 drops in a suitable liquid, and it is given before the <term>paroxysm</term> <note>a sudden attack or seizure</note> and during the paroxysm.

### *On Donkey Blood and its Essence.*
->Chap. 3.<-

From Donkey Blood, one can make an Oil or Essence in the same manner as that made from human blood. Its virtue is to heal quotidian fevers <note>fevers that recur every day</note> and quartan fevers <note>fevers that recur every fourth day, often associated with malaria</note>; it mitigates manias, frenzies, and melancholic humors <note>an excess of "black bile," believed in the 17th century to cause depression or madness</note>. ### **Spleen, and its Extract. Chap. 5.**

Take the spleen and cut it into slices; let it macerate for three days in rectified spirit of wine <term>Spirito di vino: high-proof alcohol, used here as a solvent</term> and over troglodytic myrrh <note>original: "mira trogloditic"; a high-quality variety of myrrh historically sourced from the "Troglodyte" or Red Sea coast</note>. That is, for every pound of spirit, add one ounce of myrrh. Then set the said slices to dry in the air; once they are reduced to a coarse powder, place them in a flask or matrass <term>matraccio: a long-necked glass vessel used in chemistry</term>. Pour over it enough spirit of wine so that it floats three or four fingers above the powder, placing it in a warm spot until the spirit is very well tinted. Then, pour it out gently by tilting the vessel so as not to cloud it with dregs <note>original: "feci"; the sediment or solid waste left at the bottom of a mixture</note>. Add fresh spirit again and repeat the process until it no longer takes any color. Finally, place all the tinted spirit in a flask in a water bath <note>original: "al bagno"; likely a *balneum mariae*, a gentle heating method using water</note> to distill until it reaches the consistency of an extract.

This extract is excellent for obstructions of the spleen; it resolves scirrhus <term>schiri: hard, fibrous, or cancerous swellings</term> and hardnesses. If used for forty continuous days, it consumes every bad humor <note>in early modern medicine, "humors" were bodily fluids believed to regulate health; an excess of "black bile" was often associated with the spleen</note> of that organ and makes a man feel light, as if he did not even have a spleen, so effectively does it thin it. It increases milk in women and provokes the menses; it also aids colic pains caused by hypochondriac gases <note>original: "flati hipocondriaci"; gas or "vapors" originating in the upper abdomen, often thought to cause moodiness or distress</note> and similar conditions.

The dose is from one scruple <term>scropolo: approx. 1.3 grams</term> up to one drachm <term>drama: approx. 3.9 grams</term>. Externally, the said extract, when mixed with appropriate waters or oils and applied to a place made bald by illness, makes the hair grow back <note>original: "pelli"; while literally "skins," the context of "pellato" (balded) indicates this refers to "peli" or hair</note>.

# **Of the She-Ass, and her milk. Chapter 6.**

In the absence of the aforementioned parts of the male, those of the female can be substituted, even if they are not of the same vigor in their virtues. # **The Spleen, and its Extract. Chapter 5.**

Take the spleen and cut it into slices; let it macerate for three days in rectified spirit of wine <term>Spirito di vino: high-proof distilled alcohol, often used as a solvent in alchemy</term> and over Troglodyte myrrh <note>original: "mira troglodite"; a high-quality variety of myrrh traditionally sourced from the "Troglodyte" or Red Sea coast, prized for its purity</note>; that is, for every pound of spirit, add one ounce of myrrh. Place these slices to dry in the air, and after they have been reduced to a coarse powder, place them in a flask <term>bozza: a glass vessel used in distillation</term> or matrass <term>matraccio: a long-necked glass vessel</term>. Pour over it enough spirit of wine so that it floats three or four fingers' breadth above; place it in a warm location until the spirit is well-tinted. Then, pour it out gently by tilting <note>original: "per inclinatione"; the process of decanting a liquid to separate it from the sediment</note> so as not to cloud it with the dregs <term>feci: the solid sediment or waste left after extraction</term>, and add more spirit again until it no longer takes any color. Then, place all the tinted spirit in a flask in a water bath <term>bagno: a water bath or bain-marie, used for gentle heating</term> to distill it until it reaches the consistency of an extract.

This extract is excellent for obstructions of the spleen; it dissolves scirrhi <term>schiri: hard, painless tumors or swellings, often associated with chronic congestion</term> and hardnesses. If used for forty consecutive days, it consumes every bad humor within said organ and makes a man feel light, as if he did not even have a spleen, so much does it thin it. It increases milk in women, provokes the menses, and aids colic pains caused by hypochondriac winds <note>original: "flati hipocondriaci"; gas or vapors thought to originate in the upper abdomen (the hypochondrium), often linked to melancholy or splenic distress</note> and similar conditions.

The dose is from one scruple <term>scropolo: a historical apothecary weight, approximately 1.3 grams</term> up to one drachm <term>drama: a historical apothecary weight, approximately 3.9 grams</term>. Externally, the said extract—mixed with appropriate waters or oils and applied to a spot made bald by illness—causes the hair to grow back.

### Spleen, and its Extract. Chapter 5.

# Of the Horse and its parts. Chapter 10.

From the living horse, we shall extract a most perfect extract for epilepsy <note>original: "epilepsia"</note> from the calluses <note>original: "calli." These are the horny growths on the inner side of a horse's legs, commonly known today as "chestnuts."</note> that grow on their legs. Furthermore, from the hooves of red horses that graze in the countryside where thyme, lavender, sage, savory, rosemary, and other fragrant herbs grow, one may utilize the clippings of their hooves when they are shod. From these, a Spirit, Oil, Volatile Salt, and Magistery <note>A concentrated medicinal preparation made by dissolving and then precipitating a substance.</note> shall be extracted, which will be of no less virtue <note>meaning "effectiveness" or "potency"</note> than the aforementioned remedy made from the elk's hoof.

The extract of the calluses is prepared by first drying said calluses very well. Once they are pulverized, let them be placed in a <term>fagiolo: literally "bean," referring to a bean-shaped glass vessel used in early chemistry</term>, pouring over them the Antepileptic Spirit of Wine <note>original: "Spirito di Vino Antepileptico" — a high-proof alcohol infused with medicinal herbs intended to treat seizures.</note> until it rises two or three fingers' breadth above the powder. Having sealed the vessel very well, let it be placed in <term>digestion: a process of gentle, consistent heating to extract the active properties of a substance</term> until the <term>menstruum: a solvent, in this case the alcohol, used to dissolve the medicinal components</term> is deeply colored. Then, having poured the liquid off by tilting the vessel, add more solvent until it no longer takes on any color. Once all the aforementioned Spirits have been filtered, they should be placed in a <term>bozza: a type of rounded glass flask or matrass</term> to distill until they reach the consistency of an extract.

From the dung also, by burning it and extracting its Salt—just as one extracts salt from vegetables—one will obtain a most precious Salt to provoke the menses and to expel the afterbirth <note>original: "secondine"</note> from the bodies of women in labor <note>original: "partorienti"</note>. This is administered in appropriate medicinal waters; however, the dung must be collected in the months of May and June <note>Likely because the horses would be grazing on fresh spring herbs, which was believed to increase the medicinal potency of their waste.</note>.

### Of Dung. Chapter 17.

# Excellent extract of Ox Spleen.
## Chapter 19.

Take the spleen and cut it into slices, then macerate it for two or three days in spirit of wine essentialized with Myrrh <note>original: "spirito di Vino essenzificato con Mirra" — alcohol that has been infused with the medicinal properties of myrrh resin</note>. Afterward, dry the slices and grind them coarsely into a powder. Place them in a glass vessel with enough spirit of wine so that it floats three or four finger-widths <note>original: "deta" — an informal measurement of depth</note> above the powder. Keep it in a lukewarm place until the spirit is colored. This liquid is then removed by decanting <note>original: "per inclinatione" — the act of tilting the vessel to pour off the liquid while leaving the sediment behind</note>, adding more spirit as many times as necessary until it no longer takes on color. Afterward, it is filtered and distilled until it reaches the consistency of an extract.

It is a most singular remedy for obstructions of the spleen and for provoking the menses, taking care to use it at the time they were accustomed to arrive.

The dose is one scruple <term>scruple: a unit of apothecary weight equal to 20 grains, or 1/24th of an ounce</term> in appropriate waters <note>referring to medicinal herbal waters chosen to complement the treatment</note>.

### *Of Ox Gall. Chapter 21.*

### *Essence of Ox Gall. Chapter 22.*

Take the galls and let them be dried in the sun; afterward, pour excellent spirit of wine <note>original: "spirito di vino" — high-proof distilled alcohol</note> over them, and extract a tincture or essence according to the art. To use this for the face, let it be anointed and left for three or four days; however, during that time, one must not leave the house nor be exposed to the air. After this time has passed, wash the face with water of fava bean flowers <note>original: "fiori di faua" — a common Renaissance cosmetic wash believed to soften and whiten the skin</note>, or of water lilies <note>original: "nenufari"</note>, or another. This essence also serves to remove the marks of wounds <note>scars</note>, heals ear ulcers when applied, and is excellent for earaches and deafness. It removes growths <note>original: "vngole" — literally "nails," referring here to pterygia or fleshy thickenings of the eye tissue</note> and spots from the eyes when applied for several days.

### Compound Extract of Gall. Chapter 23.

Take dried Gall <note>original: "Fiele essicato" — ox bile that has been dried into a solid or semi-solid state</note> as described above, 2 drachms <term>drachm: an apothecary unit of weight equal to 3 scruples or approximately 3.9 grams</term>.
Hepatic Aloe <note>original: "Aloè epatico" — a variety of aloe named for its liver-like color, traditionally used for digestive and liver complaints</note> }
Troglodytic Myrrh <note>original: "Mirra trogloditica" — a high-quality, fragrant resin from the Red Sea region, prized for its medicinal purity</note> } each 4 drachms.
Lesser Centaury <note>original: "Centaura minore" — a bitter herb traditionally used as a tonic to stimulate the stomach and reduce fevers</note> }

The whole shall be extracted in excellent spirit of wine <note>original: "Spirito di vino" — high-proof distilled alcohol used as a solvent</note>; a small part of this tincture can be kept aside to dissolve [blockages in] the body by wetting a cloth folded into two or three layers and applying it over the navel. Let an extract be made from the rest by distilling the spirit until it reaches a [thick] consistency, and let it be kept in a closed vessel.

The said extract is excellent for jaundice <term>jaundice (iteritia): a yellowing of the skin caused by liver or bile dysfunction</term>, hypochondria <note>Historically, this referred to physical pain or disorders of the organs located under the ribs (the hypochondrium), such as the liver or spleen</note>, dropsy <term>dropsy (hidropisia): the swelling of soft tissues due to the accumulation of excess water</term>, and tertian and quartan fevers <note>recurring fevers, common in malaria, that return every third or fourth day</note>. The dose is from half a scruple <term>scruple: a unit of weight equal to 20 grains, or about 1.3 grams</term> up to one drachm.

->ON THE STAG.<-

## THIRD SECTION

### Cap. 24.

The Stag is an animal very well known and recognized by all, both for the delightful hunt and for the frequent use of its horn—whether raw or calcined <term>Calcined: reduced to a white powder through the application of intense heat or "fire," a common process in early chemistry to extract mineral virtues</term>. Having been held in great esteem by the ancients, as it still is by modern Physicians, Chemists have therefore invented many preparations from the said horn, as well as from its various other parts. Being an animal that possesses many virtues, it is enough only to consider that it enjoys a very long life among the other quadrupeds and possesses excellent health, living for more than a hundred years. Now, the parts that serve medicine are the horns, the hide, the bone of the heart <note>original: "osso del cuore" — a small bone-like cartilage found in the hearts of stags, which was historically believed to strengthen the human heart and cure tremors</note>, the genital member, the testicles, the blood, the tears <note>likely referring to the secretions of the preorbital glands near the eyes, which were collected and used in ancient pharmacy</note>, the marrow, the tallow, the heel bone, and the stone <term>Stone: likely a "bezoar" or animal calculus, highly prized as an alexipharmic (an antidote to poison)</term>, of which things Chemistry also makes use of some, as we shall describe.

# On the Genital Organ. Chapter 34.

The genital organ of the stag is excellent for awakening the appetite of Venus <note>original: "l’appetito di Venere" — a common Renaissance euphemism for sexual desire or libido</note>, and it is beneficial for colic pains and for dysentery. It should be cooked in chervil water without being washed, and left to boil until it disintegrates. Then, the broth is strained while hot, and it will jellify upon cooling. If it is intended to awaken the appetite of Venus, it should be flavored with appropriate aromatics; similarly, for colic and dysentery, it can be made slightly acidic with spirit of vitriol <term>spirit of vitriol: a historical term for dilute sulfuric acid, used here for its astringent properties</term>, or with lemon juice, or other suitable acids.

### ->On Stag’s Blood. Chapter 36.<-
<meta>catchword: The</meta>

From the blood of a stag, and from its lungs, liver, and heart, an oil or essence is made of wonderful virtue to remove the pain, swelling, and redness of the gout <term>gout: a painful form of inflammatory arthritis, historically called "podagra" when it affected the foot</term>, and it is also excellent against poisons and contagious diseases.

It is made by taking 4 pounds of the aforementioned blood, while it is still warm, and breaking it down and dissolving it very well. The lungs, liver, and heart should be minced and placed in a large retort <term>retort: a glass vessel with a long, downward-pointing neck used for distilling substances</term>, which shall be put in a warm place to putrefy for eight days. Then, placing it in a sand bath <note>original: "in ſabbia" — a method of heating a vessel evenly by nesting it in hot sand</note>, it should first be distilled at a slow fire; afterward, the heat should be increased, and a red oil and volatile salt <term>volatile salt: a chemical salt that evaporates easily, often referring to ammonium carbonate in early pharmacy</term> will emerge, which will cling to the neck of the retort and around the receiver. This shall be separated, and the oil rectified <note>original: "rettifichi" — a process of purifying a liquid by repeated distillation</note> three or four times in a flask over sand, on top of calcothar <term>calcothar: also known as "burnt vitriol," this is the reddish iron oxide residue left after the distillation of sulfuric acid</term>, which must be changed each time. This done, the dregs <note>original: "fecci" — the solid residue left after distillation or filtration</note> should be calcined <note>original: "calcini" — heated to a high temperature to reduce a substance to powder or ash</note> until they reach whiteness. Using the "water of the blood" (which came out before the oil, having been rectified several times in a water bath <note>original: "al bagno" — a bain-marie</note> until it lost every stench), the salt shall be extracted. After distilling the water until dry, the volatile and fixed salts shall be dissolved in it once more and combined with the aforementioned oil. Leaving the whole mixture in digestion <note>original: "digeſtione" — the process of steeping a substance in gentle, consistent heat</note> for a week, all the water shall then be distilled in a water bath, and the preparation will be finished.

### On Stag’s Tears. Chapter 37.

Stag’s tears <note>likely referring to the waxy secretion from the preorbital glands of deer, which was historically prized in pharmacy</note> are cordials <term>cordial: a medicine intended to invigorate the heart and spirits</term>, comforting, and strengthening; they provoke sweating and are excellent against poisons and contagious diseases, equal to the Bezoar stone <term>Bezoar stone: a mass found in the stomachs of certain animals, believed to be a universal antidote to poison</term>. A magistery <term>magistery: a refined chemical preparation made by dissolving and then precipitating a substance into a fine powder</term> can be made from them in the same way as is done with pearls and corals.

The dose is from three grains to four or five.

### On Stag Fat and Tallow. Chapter 38.

An oil is also made from stag fat by distillation in the same manner as that of butter; therefore, let one refer to its specific chapter.

It has the power to soften and soothe, and it marvelously eases the pains of sciatica <term>sciatica: nerve pain affecting the back, hip, and leg</term>, gout <term>podagra: the historical name for gout, specifically when it affects the foot</term>, and other similar conditions by anointing the area once or twice a day.

### On the Astragalus, and the stones found in the heart of the Stag. Chapter 39.

The Astragalus <note>original: "Astragallo" — the talus or ankle bone of a deer, historically used in various preparations</note>, which is reduced to a magistery <term>magistery: a refined chemical preparation made by dissolving and then precipitating a substance into a fine powder</term> by calcining it <term>calcination: the process of heating a substance to high temperatures to reduce it to a friable powder</term> and extracting it with distilled vinegar, then precipitating it with oil of Tartar <term>oil of Tartar: a saturated solution of potassium carbonate, used as a chemical reagent</term>.

The said magistery is excellent for suffocation of the mother <term>suffocation of the mother: a historical medical term for hysteria or respiratory distress believed to be caused by the womb</term>, and it assists women in labor; it also benefits those who have ingested poisons.

The dose is from six grains to one scruple <term>scruple: a unit of apothecary weight, approximately 1.3 grams</term>.

The powder or ash that remains is excellent for dysentery <term>dysentery: an inflammatory infection of the intestines</term>.

The dose is one drachm <term>drachm: an apothecary weight, approximately 3.9 grams</term> in appropriate liquids.

The stone that is found in the heart of the Stag has the same virtues as the Bezoar stone <term>Bezoar stone: a hard mass found in the digestive systems of animals, highly prized as a universal antidote to poison</term>.
