### Of the Wild-Goat, or the Animal that Produces the Bezoar Stone. Chapter 42.

**The Wild-Goat** <term>Wild-Goat: original "Capriceruo," literally "Goat-Stag," likely referring to the ibex or other mountain ruminants</term> is an animal which is found in Persia, and in the East Indies, and in Peru, and in New Spain <note>The Spanish colonial territory including modern-day Mexico and Central America</note>; it is in part similar to the Deer, and in part similar to the Wild Goat, or Chamois <term>Chamois: original "Camossa," a species of mountain goat-antelope</term>. Nature has given this animal the property of generating a stone in its intestines, which is the most excellent remedy against poisons. Those stones extracted from oriental animals, such as from the countries of the East Indies, possess the greatest virtue; in second place follow those from Peru, and after those from New Spain, which are the most inferior. From this stone one can extract salt, magistery <term>magistery: in alchemy, a master-preparation or a concentrated extract of a substance's essential properties</term>, essence, and other things, just as with Pearls and other similar substances.

# Of the Wolf. Chapter 45.

## Of the Wolf. Chapter 45.

Since the Wolf is a wild dog, I wanted to place him in this section; many things can be made from him which are very useful for various infirmities. First, an extract is made from the dried heart; it is an excellent remedy for the falling sickness <term>falling sickness: original "mal caduco," a historical term for epilepsy</term>, when prepared with anti-epileptic spirit of wine <term>spirit of wine: high-proof alcohol used as a medicinal solvent</term>. Similarly, from its liver, also dried, an extract is made with spirit of wine which is a specific remedy for those with lung disease <term>lung disease: original "polmonisti," referring to those suffering from pulmonary conditions such as tuberculosis</term> and dropsy <term>dropsy: original "hidropici," an old term for edema or swelling caused by fluid retention</term>. From the calcined intestines, reduced to a magistery <term>magistery: original "magistero," a refined medicinal substance or precipitate prepared through chemical processes</term>, one gives the weight of a scruple <term>scruple: a small unit of weight used by apothecaries, roughly 1.3 grams</term> for colic pains. The dung similarly has the same virtue when reduced to a magistery. From the bones, a magistery is also made which is excellent for pleurisy <term>pleurisy: original "pleurisia," an inflammation of the lungs' lining that causes sharp chest pain</term>. From the blood, an essence is made—as was described regarding the blood of the Deer—which is good for coagulated blood. Finally, an oil is made from the fat of the Wolf, which is excellent for gouty pains <term>gouty: original "podagrici," referring to podagra or gout, particularly in the joints of the feet</term>.

### Of the Cat. Chapter 47.

From the fat Cat, particularly the wild one, an oil or fat is made of marvelous virtue for any kind of joint pain, even if they are long-standing <term>long-standing: original "inveterate," referring to chronic or deep-seated conditions</term>. ### *Virtues of the water, or spirit of Fox.*

The aforementioned water or spirit, taken in a dose of approximately two ounces <note>original: "due onzie"</note>, possesses all the virtues mentioned above, but is particularly effective for stones <note>kidney or bladder stones</note> and difficulty urinating. It is even more effective than the essence for the bite of a rabid dog; both the water and the essence should be taken internally and applied to the injured part after performing the necessary scarifications <term>scarifications: small incisions made in the skin to draw out "tainted" blood or venom</term> and applying cupping glasses <term>cupping glasses: "ventose," tools used to create suction over a wound to draw out toxins</term> over the wounds.

It should be noted that during the aforementioned distillation, a volatile salt <term>volatile salt: a chemical substance, often ammonium carbonate in animal-based preparations, that vaporizes easily</term> will emerge. This should be combined with the spirit or water through the process of digestion <note>digestion: a process of prolonged, gentle heating used to combine substances</note>. It would also be appropriate to calcine <term>calcine: to burn a substance until it is reduced to ash or powder</term> the dregs <note>original: "fecci"</note> remaining in the vessel <note>original: "orinale," referring to the urinal-shaped glass vessel used in the lab</note> and extract their salt, which should then be joined with the aforementioned water.

From the skin, an oil can be extracted through distillation; this also causes hair to regrow.

### Furnace for descent with its distilling vessels.

**A** Furnace.

But even though it is so ferocious and untamed, it is caught with great ease—as some report—because it goes by its own accord to place itself in the lap of a Virgin, and falling asleep there, the hunters take it at their pleasure. ### Of the Elephant; Chapter 53.

Having spoken of the **Rhinoceros**, we shall now discuss one of its mortal enemies, which is the **Elephant**. Among all wild animals, this is the most docile and pleasant to be found; it seems to possess a certain particular understanding, for when it must be loaded onto a ship (as some report), those who lead it must promise under oath to return it to the place where they took it. It is a very lively animal and has a very long and mobile nose, made in the shape of a **Trumpet** <note>original: "Tromba," referring to the trunk</note>, with which it takes the food it wishes to eat and places it in its mouth. It has enormous strength in this nose, for it can take a man or a heavy load and place it upon its shoulders or back. It is also so strong that the ancients used them in **War**, loading a wooden tower onto their backs, inside of which stood a squad of men who fought with bows and arrows.

Among all parts of the said animal, none is more useful, better known, or more common than its tooth, which is called **Ivory** by the common people.

# SIXTH SECTION.
## Chapter 56.

This name "Serpents" in general refers to many species; but here it must be noted that I intend to speak of no other than vipers, as they are the most effective <note>original: "virtuose"; in early modern science, this refers to the inherent power or "virtue" of a medicinal substance</note> and health-giving. It is true that if one cannot obtain them, one may take in their place those terrestrial snakes <note>original: "colobre"; likely referring to snakes of the Colubridae family, which are generally non-venomous</note> that are of the same color, but even so, the preparations will never have as much potency as those made from the viper. Among so many species of serpents, only the viper gives birth to its young alive, which is where the name **Viper** <note>The author is referring to the traditional etymology of *vipera*, derived from the Latin *vivus* (alive) and *parere* (to bring forth)</note> is derived. Eggs form within the body of the viper, and as the time of birth approaches, they hatch inside her body; afterward, she gives birth to live little vipers, numbering eight, nine, or even up to twelve. I have seen this in Milan, and also in Bologna in an apothecary shop <note>original: "spetiaria"; a pharmacy that also sold spices and chemical ingredients</note>, where a viper gave birth to twelve little vipers; I saw them all alive, and the mother as well. This is contrary to those sophisticated inventors of new things who claim that when these little vipers are born, they gnaw through the mother's belly, and thus she must die. ## Preparation of the Viper, and the way to make Animal Bezoar, or Viperine powder in several ways.

->Chapter 57.<-

One should take the vipers caught at the beginning of Spring, but not immediately upon the end of Winter; rather, let us say, in mid-April, more or less according to the current weather. Ensure they are young females and are not pregnant. By cutting off their head and tail, they are skinned, and the innards and fat are removed. After rinsing them in Malmsey wine <note>original: "maluasia"; a sweet, potent wine frequently used in early modern pharmacy for its cleansing and preservative qualities</note>, they are washed and set to dry in the air so that they do not touch one another. Once they are dry, to make the simple Animal Bezoar <note>While "Bezoar" usually refers to a stone found in the stomach of a goat, the author uses it here to describe a potent medicinal powder derived from animal remains</note>, they are pulverized along with the vertebrae and everything else, and the powder is kept for use.

The dose is from half a drachm <note>a historical unit of weight; half a drachm is approximately 1.9 grams</note> to one.

### Essence of Vipers. Chapter 62.

Take the livers and hearts of vipers in equal parts <note>original: "ana" — a medical shorthand meaning "of each an equal amount."</note>, as much as can be obtained. Having dried them in a <term>stove</term> <note>A drying oven or heated chamber used by pharmacists to remove moisture from organic materials.</note>, they are pulverized and then placed in <term>vessels</term> <note>The original text "fagioli" (beans) is likely a transcription error or an archaic term for bean-shaped glass vessels or vials.</note>. Place it in <term>digestion</term> <note>The process of steeping a substance in a liquid with gentle heat to extract its medicinal properties.</note> for three or four days until the tincture has been extracted. Then, pour it off by <term>decanting</term> <note>original: "votarà per inclinatione" — tilting the vessel to pour out the liquid while leaving the sediment behind.</note>, and squeeze and filter the whole mixture. To every eight ounces of this Essence, add one ounce of fixed volatile salt, and place it in digestion in a <term>warm water bath</term> <note>A bain-marie; heating a vessel inside another container of water to ensure gentle, even heat.</note> for forty days, and it will be finished.

Its virtues are similar to those mentioned above for the fixed volatile salt.
The dose is from one scruple up to one <term>drachm</term> <note>An apothecary weight equal to 3 scruples, or about 3.9 grams.</note>, or more.

### Of the Civet Cat. Chapter 66.

The <term>Civet Cat</term> <note>Despite the name, civets are not cats but Viverrids, small carnivores native to Africa and Asia. They were highly prized in the early modern period for their aromatic secretions.</note> is a foreign animal, but sometimes some are brought here by people out of curiosity; a few years ago one was seen in Genoa, and another in Milan. Civet is the <term>sweat</term> <note>While described here as sweat, civet is actually a glandular secretion from the perineal glands. They then go about collecting it by scraping it off with a small piece of <term>lantern horn</term> <note>A thin, translucent slice of animal horn used in lantern panes before glass became common; here used as a flexible spatula.</note> or other similar object.

Civet is hot and moist in temperament; it is helpful when applied to headaches caused by a cold nature, it strengthens the brain, and it is excellent for colic pains by anointing the navel. It is also good for the bodily pains of childbirth and for <term>suffocation of the mother</term> <note>A historical medical term (Latin: *strangulatio vulvae*) for what was later called hysteria; it was believed the womb could physically shift upward and cause a sense of choking.</note> when applied to the opening of the navel; likewise, to draw the womb back down during such a suffocation, it can be applied to the <term>mouth of nature</term> <note>A common early modern euphemism for the vagina.</note>.

With <term>Spirit of Wine</term> <note>High-proof alcohol, often produced by distilling wine.</note>, a tincture or essence of civet is extracted, which is excellent for strengthening the brain and creating a good memory. It is also helpful for apoplexy, paralysis, epilepsy, convulsions, and the like, by taking a few drops in an appropriate <term>vehicle</term> <note>A liquid such as water, wine, or broth used to dilute and administer a medicine.</note> and by anointing the afflicted part.

# ON THE HEN,
# Rooster, Turkey,
## and their species.

### FIRST QUARTER.

#### Chapter 1.

I shall begin this book by starting with the Hen, an animal very well known to everyone; and if we wish to consider a great act of provident nature toward man, let us consider for a moment how she has endowed this little creature with the faculty of producing such a great quantity of eggs. This is something no other animal does, for others only produce a certain amount to maintain their generation <note>meaning their lineage or the survival of the species</note>; but Hens lay them continually, almost every day. This is because the Supreme Provider <note>a reference to God as the ultimate source of natural order</note> has had regard for the great utility that man derives from them in his infirmities and in cases of weakness, there being for the most part no food more suitable than fresh eggs. Furthermore, eggs are used in such a variety of foods that there is not a day in which an immense quantity is not consumed; and for the use of medicine they have an infinity of virtues <term>virtues: the inherent medicinal or healing powers believed to reside within a natural substance</term>, as we shall mention some in their proper place. Take an old, healthy hen, plucked and cleaned; cut it into small pieces. Together with a **suckling calf's** <term>suckling calf: a young calf still fed on milk, used here because its feet are rich in the collagen needed to make gelatin</term> foot, set it to boil for eight hours with a sufficient quantity of spring water in a very well-covered **pot** <term>pot: 'pignata', a traditional deep earthenware cooking vessel</term>. After straining the broth and pressing the meat, flavor it to taste with those spices that will be found appropriate for the sick person. If desired, add a little lemon juice as well, and place it to set in a cold place. This is an outstanding **nutrient** and **tonic** <term>tonic: 'corroborativo', a substance intended to strengthen or invigorate the body's systems</term>, and it comforts the stomach.

A hen juice, or **pesto** <note>original: 'pesto', meaning a preparation that has been pounded or crushed with a mortar and pestle</note>, is also made for the nourishment of the sick by cooking the hen until the meat falls away from the bones on its own, then pounding everything very well—

## *Of the Turkey Hen and Cock*
### *Chapt. 7.*

Those which we call *Turkeys* <note>original: 'Galline d' India' (Hens of India). In the 16th and 17th centuries, turkeys were frequently called 'Hens of India' because they originated in the Americas, then known as the 'West Indies'</note> differ little in their properties <note>original: 'virtù'—referring to the medicinal or nutritional power of the animal</note> from those of the *Hen*. Thus, when they are young, they may also be permitted to the sick in place of *local hens*. It is indeed true, however, that once they are fully grown and are no longer *pullets* <note>young hens</note>, they are of a warmer temperament <term>Temperament: in Galenic medicine, this refers to the balance of the four humors (hot, cold, moist, dry)</term> and a denser substance than our *Hens*. Consequently, they are harder to digest, not differing much from the nature of the *Goose* <note>original: 'Occa', an archaic spelling of 'oca'</note>. Therefore, their fat is of a moderate temperament, falling between that of the *Hen* and the *Goose*, and is consequently similar in its properties. Their eggs provide good nourishment, though they are a little harder to digest than those of *local hens*. In conclusion, they are similar in properties, and one may utilize from them all that we have said regarding the *Hen* and its parts in its absence.

## Of the Partridge. Chapt. 9.

Among our local Birds, both domestic and wild, the **Partridge** is the most lively of all; and no sooner are the chicks born than they walk with such great speed that a good warhorse <note>original: 'Destriero'—a powerful, spirited horse used in battle or tournaments</note> would have difficulty following them. Certainly, among foods of good substance, the Partridge holds first place, both for the good temperament that constitutes its nature—it living for a quite long time—and for the goodness, flavor, and substance of its meat. ### Concerning Turtle Doves. Chapt. 114

The Turtle dove, a very well-known bird, teaches us how those joined in **marriage** should conduct themselves. It loves its dear companion so dearly that, should the mate be lost, it lives in such loathing that it truly can be said to despise living in the world. It perches only on dry trees and branches, wanting us to understand that all hope is lost for it. It never eats unless driven by great necessity, and even then, only enough to survive. It flees all other company, mourning continually for the loss of its dear companion. In short, it shows us that it would value meeting death more than living in such a tearful state—all of which should bring shame to those men and

## Of Quails. Chapter 12.

The **Quail** is a bird well-known enough, yet very little used in medicine; it is indeed true that those of the fields, which feed on **Hellebore** <note>A toxic plant; quails were famously believed in antiquity to be immune to its poison, though humans could be poisoned by eating birds that had consumed it</note>, boiled and eaten, move the bowels <note>original: 'mouono il corpo', a common medical euphemism for laxative effects</note>, purge the kidneys, and help with their pains. The fat of the **Quail** is beneficial when applied to spots on the eyes <note>Likely referring to cataracts or corneal scarring</note>; but it is much better to make the following ointment: **Quail** fat, 2 drachms <term>Drachm: an apothecary weight, roughly 3.9 grams</term>; virgin honey, myrrh, and Cyprian vitriol <note>original: 'Vitriolo di Cipriana'. This refers to copper sulfate, historically sourced from Cyprus and used as an astringent and antiseptic</note>, 1 drachm of each. Let it be mixed into the form of an ointment and applied every other day to the afflicted eyes, until the spots have disappeared. Furthermore, the excrement of the aforementioned **Quails**, taken by mouth, is a specific remedy for the falling sickness <term>Falling sickness: a historical name for epilepsy</term>. It should be cautioned that those who suffer from spasmodic pains <note>original: 'dolori spasmatici', referring to cramps or convulsions</note> should not eat **Quails** unless they have first been purged and kept for a long time in the house, because those that have eaten **Hellebore** are harmful to them.

# ON THRUSHES, BLACKBIRDS,
## And other Birds.

### THIRD QUARTER
#### Chapter 13.

**Thrushes** and **Blackbirds** provide excellent nourishment and are easily digested; being fatty, they are beneficial to those with hectic fevers <term>Hectic fever: a lingering, recurring fever often associated with "wasting" diseases like tuberculosis</term> and the emaciated. ### Concerning the Lark: Chapter 16.

There are two species of the Lark, called by the Latins *Alauda* <note>original: 'Alauda'</note>: the common one—that is, the one with a crest—which we properly call the Lark, and the other without a crest, which we call the Calandra. The first is superior in its medicinal virtues to the second. Its heart, bound to the body, removes colic pain; therefore, it is useful for those who suffer from it to carry it. Similarly, the said heart is excellent when eaten fresh. The bird is also prepared by being burned to ashes whole with its feathers; by giving one to two spoonfuls of this powder for several days, it heals every sort of colic, however severe they may be.

The fresh blood, drunk with a sharp <note>original: 'brusco'; referring to a dry or tart wine</note> white wine or with vinegar, is wonderfully helpful to those who suffer from stones <note>original: 'calcoli'; kidney or bladder stones</note>.

# CONCERNING THE DUCK, GOOSE, AND PEACOCK.

## FOURTH SECTION.

### Chapter 18.

In this section we will discuss the Duck, the Goose, and the Peacock—animals well known to everyone—and in this chapter we will speak of the Duck, both domestic and wild. Both are of a hot temperament <note>According to the humoral theory of medicine, "hot" substances were used to counteract "cold" illnesses</note>; they digest even stones, and their meat is of heavy substance and difficult to digest. The fat is moisturizing, digestive, and emollient, and for this reason it is good in <term>pessaries</term> <note>medical plugs or suppositories used for localized internal treatment</note> for hardness of the womb. It heals cracks in the face and hands caused by the cold, and it softens hard areas of the breasts and the genitals. This fat, when cooked inside an onion or fried within one, heals ear pain and removes water from the ears when dripped in while warm.

The blood is counted among the <term>alexipharmics</term> <note>original: 'Alexifarmaci'; from the Greek for 'warding off poison,' these were substances used as antidotes</note>, and it is excellent against the poison of the <term>sea hare</term> <note>original: 'lepre marcino' (marino); a type of sea slug or mollusk that ancient and medieval naturalists believed was deadly if touched or eaten</note>.

An excellent oil is made from duck fat for sciatic pain and for cold gout, as follows.

### Of the Goose. Cap. 19.

The Goose is a very well-known animal; its meat is difficult to digest, generating melancholic humors <note>In the humoral theory of medicine, "black bile" or melancholy was associated with heaviness and depression; foods that produced it were often considered unhealthy for regular consumption</note>, therefore its use is not highly praised. Its fat is more subtle and penetrating; for this reason, it resolves hardness <note>softens inflammatory swellings or tumors</note>, and it is good for noises and pains in the ears. When drunk, it is an excellent remedy for those who have taken cantharides <note>original: 'cantaride'; Spanish Fly, a toxic beetle often used as a stimulant or blister agent that could cause severe internal poisoning</note>.

The blood of the Goose is also an <term>alexipharmic</term> <note>a medicine used to ward off or treat the effects of poison</note> against venoms, just like that of the Duck.

Goose dung, when mixed with ripening medications <note>remedies designed to draw out or "ripen" an infection</note>, causes <term>apostemes</term> <note>original: 'posteme'; a historical term for an abscess or large swelling filled with purulent matter</note> to break open.

---

### Of the Peacock. Cap. 20.

The Peacock is the most beautiful animal we have in our region, and among all our domestic animals, it is the one with the longest life, being able to surpass thirty years. For this reason, its meat is of a balsamic nature <note>meaning it has preservative qualities; it was a common early modern belief that peacock meat did not decay as quickly as other meats</note>, possessing a vigorous strength and substance, and it remains preserved without spoiling for entire months.

The broth made from its meat is excellent for pleurisy <note>an inflammation of the membranes surrounding the lungs</note>, particularly when the bird is fat and the broth is given warm to the patient.

The <term>songia</term> <note>original: 'songia'; refers to the internal leaf fat or grease of the animal, often used as a base for ointments</note> of a Peacock, mixed with the juice of Rue <note>original: 'Rutta'; a bitter herb (*Ruta graveolens*) used widely in traditional medicine</note> and honey, excellently heals colicky pains.

### Of the Crane. Cap. 22.

THE Crane is an animal of a very sinewy <note>original: 'neruoso'; in early medicine, this described both the nervous system and the physical tendons or sinews</note> nature, and therefore it benefits the effects of the nerves; its fat is marvelous for pains of the same (that is, of the nerves) even if they are long-standing. It is also excellent for earaches when distilled into them; and when mixed with gum ammoniac <note>a medicinal resin derived from a flowering plant in the carrot family, used as a stimulant and to treat swelling</note>, it dissolves the stubborn hardness of the spleen, as well as other tumors such as hernias and the like, softening all their hardness.

Its meat, eaten by those who suffer from colic pains <note>severe, fluctuating abdominal pain</note>, even if long-standing, is said to be an admirable remedy.

Its heart, eaten by epileptics, benefits them greatly.

Its gall <note>original: 'fiele'; bile used in early medicine for its supposed "cutting" or "cleansing" properties</note>, distilled into the eyes, removes dimness and clouds <note>likely referring to cataracts or corneal opacities</note>.

The head with the eyes, and the gizzard <note>original: 'ventricolo'</note>, dried and powdered, are good for ulcers, fistulas <note>abnormal passages or holes in the body caused by infection</note>, cancers <note>original: 'cancheri'; used historically to describe persistent, eating sores or malignant growths</note>, and various other things.

### Of the Raven. Cap. 23.

Among the animals of our lands, there is no animal of longer life than the Raven, which many report lives up to three hundred years and more. From young ravens, one can make a water against the falling sickness <note>original: 'morbo caduco'; an early name for epilepsy</note>, similar to that made from the Magpie <note>original: 'Gaza'</note>, and it is marvelous. Also admirable are the aforementioned chicks when dried in a pot in the oven and powdered; given at the weight of one dram <note>a traditional unit of apothecary weight, roughly 3.9 grams</note> to the patient for several days, they will be healed. The same ash benefits those who suffer from arthritic <note>original: 'artetici'</note> and gouty <note>original: 'podagrici'</note> pains. Eating one or two raven eggs, hard-boiled in vinegar, cures dysentery.

The dung of the Raven, placed in a decayed tooth, eases its pain and makes it fall out little by little.

### Of the Stork. Cap. 24.

The Stork feeds on snakes, and for this reason it is numbered among the alexipharmics <note>from the Greek 'alexipharmakon', referring to an antidote or a remedy that protects against poison or infection</note> of no small importance. As many authors report, it is effective against every kind of poison; when eaten, it serves as a great preservative against the plague, and it benefits those with paralysis, spasms, arthritis, and other conditions of the nerves. Crollius <note>Oswald Croll (c. 1563–1609), a famous German iatrochemist and physician who advocated for chemical medicines</note> composes a universal alexipharmic from it, which I did not want to omit including here.

# ON THE EEL, Pike, Tench, Perch, and Trout.

## FIRST QUARTER.

### Chapter I.

The Eel is a very delicate food, but hard to digest, viscous, and harmful to those who suffer from illnesses proceeding from <term>catarrh: an early medical term for an excess of phlegm or mucus in the body's airways or cavities</term>. However, if it is eaten, it is of less harm when cooked on a spit; and the fat that drips from it is excellent for deafness of the ears when applied to them. Or, as some prefer, one may cook several cloves of Garlic in it, and then place them into the patient's ear in the form of a <term>plug: "tasta" in the original, referring to a small wad of linen or a medicinal wick used to deliver treatment into an orifice</term>.

The aforementioned fat is good for promoting hair growth and cures <term>alopecia: the medical condition of hair loss</term>, that is, for those whose hair is falling out; it also relieves the pain of hemorrhoids and dissolves <term>scrofulous glands: swollen lymph nodes, historically often associated with tuberculosis or the "King's Evil"</term>.

If you cut off the head of an Eel and, while it is still bleeding, rub it on <term>warts: "porri" in Italian, which literally means leeks, but in a medical context refers to skin growths or warts</term>, and then bury the head in the ground to rot, they say it causes the said warts to fall off.

The blood of the Eel, while warm—that is, freshly drawn—drunk in wine, helps with <term>colic: severe, cramping pains in the abdomen</term>.

Many report that wine in which an eel has been drowned, when given to drink, causes the person who drinks it to completely loathe wine. <note>This was a common folk remedy for alcoholism in the early modern period.</note>

### On the Pike. Chapter 2.

The gall of the Pike is so miraculous for ailments of the eyes that it restores sight lost due to cataracts, by placing it over them and leaving it for twenty-four hours; this has led many to believe that the fish which the Angel commanded the young Tobias to catch was of this species. <note>Referring to the Book of Tobit in the Apocrypha, where the Archangel Raphael instructs Tobias to use the gall of a fish to heal his father's blindness.</note>

Pike gall is also excellent for removing calluses on the toes when applied to them; and when drunk in an appropriate <term>vehicle: a liquid substance, such as water, wine, or syrup, used to administer a medicine</term>, it helps with fevers, as does eating the heart.

The jawbone of the Pike, reduced to powder, is a specific remedy for <term>pleurisy: a painful inflammation of the membranes surrounding the lungs</term> when given in the weight of one <term>scruple: a small historical unit of apothecary weight, roughly 1.3 grams</term> up to one <term>drachm: an ancient unit of weight equal to about 3.9 grams</term>.

The aforementioned jawbone, along with the other bones of the head, reduced to powder or made into a <term>magistery: a high-quality medicinal preparation or extract made according to the specialized rules of pharmacy or alchemy</term> according to the art, is a great remedy for <term>the stone: a common historical term for kidney or bladder stones</term>; it is also excellent for the <term>white flow: historically known as leucorrhea, a discharge from the female reproductive tract</term>.

Pike roe purges the body and sometimes induces vomiting, and for this reason, they are employed as a medicine.

### On the Tench. Chapter 3.

Truly wonderful are the effects of Nature; while we see marvelous things produced by causes unknown to us, differing from their known humors, this is what has led some to say that such things operate through an **occult property** <note>In early modern science, "occult properties" referred to natural powers that were observable but whose underlying mechanisms could not be explained by the standard theory of the four humors.</note>, as one cannot provide a clear reason for their actions. This is exactly what happens with the **Tench**, which—though a fish of a cold and moist <term>temperament: the balance of the four bodily humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) believed to determine health and personality</term>—is able to attract the humor that generates **Jaundice**, which is normally an action associated with heat.

As many claim, if the fish is tied alive over the patient's navel and left until it is dead, and if this process is repeated three times (that is, using two more live Tench), the third fish will turn entirely yellow. This is because it has drawn into itself the yellowness of the jaundiced patient, who will then remain healed.

The aforementioned fish, split down the middle and placed on the wrists and the soles of the feet, helps to mitigate the great heat of burning and malignant fevers, and diverts pestilential poison.

Reduced to ash, it is excellent for the <term>white flows: historically known as leukorrhea, a medical term for vaginal discharge</term> of women.

Its gall <note>The bile or "fielle" was frequently used in ancient and Renaissance medicine for its perceived sharp, cleansing properties.</note> helps with deafness of the ears.

In its head, there is a triangular stone which aids in <term>colic: severe, fluctuating pain in the abdomen</term> and <term>nephritic: relating to the kidneys, often referring to kidney stones</term> pains; it also helps with the <term>falling sickness: an archaic term for epilepsy</term>, especially when reduced into a <term>magistery: a high-quality medicinal preparation or extract made according to specialized rules of pharmacy or alchemy</term> in the same manner as one makes a magistery from <term>crab's eyes: small, stony concretions (gastroliths) found in the stomachs of crayfish, used in early medicine to treat various ailments</term>.

### *On the Perch. Chapter 4.*

Among the fish considered healthy for food, the **Perch**, or *Perca*, does not hold the lowest rank. Within its head, one finds a stone which is excellent for the <term>sickness of the stone: a historical term for urinary calculi, such as kidney or bladder stones</term>. Some further claim that wearing the stone found in the head of a sea Perch upon one's person greatly assists those who suffer from **nephritic pains** <note>original: "dolori nefretici"; refers to intense pain caused by kidney stones or inflammation.</note>.

### *On the Trout. Chapter 5.*

It is not necessary to tell anyone how much the **Trout** is esteemed at the table, for this is known to everyone. This reputation is not without reason, as it is a fish of excellent substance that generates **good juice** <term>good juice: also called "good chyme," this refers to the high-quality fluids produced during digestion which were thought to create healthy blood and humors</term>. While it is of most excellent taste, it is true that it is little used in medicine, except for its fat, which serves to heal **rhagades**, or rather, fissures of the fundament <note>original: "ragadie, ò sia fissure del sedere." Rhagades are painful cracks or linear scars in the skin or mucous membranes, often occurring around the anus.</note>.

# ON THE BARBEL, CARP, GUDGEON, AND LAMPREY.

## SECOND SECTION.

### Chapter 6.

The **Barbel** is a very well-known fish, and little of it is used in medicine, although its eggs <note>original: "oua"; referring here to the fish roe.</note> produce the same effect as <term>emetic Antimony: a chemical compound used historically to induce vigorous vomiting and purging of the bowels</term>, purging from both above and below, and with such violence that many times those who eat them are in danger of their lives, and some have died. This effect occurs more violently in the Spring, when they eat the **willow flowers**; therefore, let everyone be careful, because at such a time they are pernicious.

### On the Carp. Chapter 7.

The **Carp**, or as we call it, the **Queen fish** <note>original: "pesce Regina."</note>, is well known to everyone. Its **gall** is helpful for clouds <note>original: "nuuole"; likely referring to cataracts or corneal opacities that dim the vision.</note> and watering of the eyes. There is found in its head a **triangular stone**, similar to that of the **Tench**, which is excellent for all things, as we have said regarding those of the Tench <note>The previous page noted that stones from a fish's head were used to treat "the sickness of the stone," or urinary calculi.</note>.

Its fat is a most exquisite remedy for pains of the nerves caused by <term>heat: in the humeral system of medicine, an excess of the quality of "calidity" (heat) was thought to cause specific types of inflammation and pain</term>.

# ON THE CRAYFISH,
## Frog, and Tortoise.

->THIRD SECTION.<-

->Chap. 10.<-

Local **Crayfish** <note>original: "Gambari"; while the term can refer to shrimp, in this context of river animals, it refers to freshwater crayfish.</note> are very useful in medicine, and there is no part of them that is not beneficial and used for various effects. Whether used whole and potent, or reduced to powder, they serve as an excellent remedy against the **bite of a rabid dog**, when given with an equal weight of powdered **gentian root**, in the dose of one <term>dram: an apothecary unit of weight, approximately 3.9 grams</term> for forty consecutive days.

The **ash** of these same creatures is used for **cracked feet** caused by the cold, when mixed with **honey** in the form of an ointment and applied upon them.

The aforementioned **Crab** <note>original: "Granchio"; the author uses this term here interchangeably with crayfish, likely referring to the freshwater river crab or the general class of crustaceans.</note>, when eaten, benefits those suffering from **consumption** <note>original: "Tifici"; a historical term for those suffering from tuberculosis or similar wasting diseases characterized by "hectic" fever.</note>; it soothes pain, cools, and hydrates. One should note that it must be **boiled**, eating the meat and drinking the broth; and **Paul of Aegina** <note>original: "Paolo Aetio"; a renowned 7th-century Byzantine Greek physician known for his medical encyclopedia.</note> says it is effective against poison, and the bites or stings of venomous animals.

A water is also **distilled** from the Crayfish, which is excellent for quenching thirst in burning fevers, and it drives out **retained urine**, driv-

-ing out stones and gravel. Take young **Crayfish**, crush them, and place them to **distill** in a <term>bain-marie: a water bath used for gentle heating</term>; what remains is dried and made into a powder, or otherwise **calcined** <note>original: "calcina"; the process of heating a substance to high temperatures to reduce it to a friable powder.</note> to serve the aforementioned purpose.

**Crayfish eyes** <note>original: "occhi di Gambari"; these are not actually eyes, but "gastroliths"—small stones of calcium carbonate found in the stomachs of crayfish, highly prized in early modern medicine as antacids.</note> cool, dry, cleanse, disperse, and destroy **stones**, promote the flow of urine, and are excellent for **kidney pains**. They benefit **pleurisy** by absorbing the acid that causes the ailment, and are excellent for **asthma** and **colic pains**. They dissolve clotted blood and **tartar** <note>original: "tartaro"; in this medical context, it refers to stony deposits within the body's vessels or organs.</note>. They are taken reduced to a powder, or in a <term>magistery: a refined medicinal precipitate or "master" preparation of a substance</term>. This is made by taking the crayfish eyes reduced to powder and placing them inside a <term>matrass: a round-bottomed glass flask with a long neck, used in distilling</term> with good distilled vinegar so that it sits three or four fingers' depth above them. Leave it until the bubbling stops and the vinegar has dissolved all it can; then, pour it off by tilting the flask. Add more vinegar until no more dissolves. All these vinegars are then filtered. Once filtered, drop **Oil of Tartar** <note>original: "oglio di Tartaro fatto per deliquio"; a solution of potassium carbonate created by letting the salt absorb moisture from the air until it liquefies.</note> onto them drop by drop until the entire magistery has **precipitated** and settled to the bottom. After pouring off the extra liquid, wash it several times with water to remove any saltiness. Finally, wash it with a **cordial water** <note>a medicinal water intended to invigorate the heart or spirit</note> and store it for use.

The **dose** is from six to eight **grains** <note>an apothecary unit of weight, roughly 65 milligrams</note> up to 20.

Of the **powder**, the dose is from half a <term>scruple: an apothecary weight of about 1.3 grams</term> up to half a <term>dram: an apothecary unit of weight, approximately 3.9 grams</term>.

### **Of Frogs. Chapter II.**

Here I intend to speak of aquatic **Frogs**, that is, those that we use for food, as the others are rather useless in medicine than good; however, in speaking of the **Frog**, we shall refer particularly to the **river-dwelling** ones, which truly possess very great virtues. There is no part of them that does not serve a purpose or is useless to medicine. We shall say, therefore, that **Dioscorides** <note>Pedanius Dioscorides (c. 40–90 AD), a Greek physician and botanist whose work *De Materia Medica* was the primary pharmacological text for 1,500 years.</note> provides it as an **Antidote** against the venom of any snake whatsoever, by eating them cooked with oil and salt and drinking their broth. Similarly, they also benefit those who suffer from pains in the body due to trapped winds caused by thick and viscous excrement.

The said **Frogs**, taken alive in this way and placed on the wrists of the arms and on the side where the heart passes <note>The author refers to placing the frog on pulse points or the left side of the chest to "cool" the blood.</note>, mitigate the great heat of burning fevers. Similarly, when placed over **carbuncles** <note>original: "antracie"; severe, deep-seated sores or boils.</note> or **pestilential buboes**, they draw out their poison. They similarly benefit **Saint Anthony’s fire** <note>original: "fuoco sacro"; a skin condition, likely shingles or ergotism, characterized by a burning sensation.</note> and **erysipelas** <note>original: "eresipile"; a bacterial skin infection causing large, red, inflamed patches.</note>. ### On the Turtle. Chapter 12.

The **turtle** is of two species, aquatic and terrestrial; but both are very beneficial in their virtues. They provide excellent nourishment and are a superb food for those who suffer from the early stages of **hectic fever** <note>original: "hetica"; a historical term for a chronic, wasting fever, often associated with the early stages of tuberculosis or consumption.</note>. The terrestrial turtle is particularly suited for this purpose.

### Of the Sturgeon. Cap. 13.

The **Sturgeon** is a fish that lives in rivers and in the sea as well; it is a more delicate food than any other fish common to us, though in medicine it is little used. Its bones, dried and pulverized, are excellent for curing **wandering arthritis** <term>artretide vaga: a historical term for joint pain or gout that moves from one part of the body to another.</term>, as well as for dispersing the **winds** <note>flatulence or internal gases</note> that generate **colic pains**.

### Of the Cuttlefish. Cap. 15.

Regarding the **Cuttlefish** <note>original: "Scepia"</note>, among all its parts, the **bones** <note>cuttlebone</note> are in great use; **goldsmiths** use them to cast rings, crosses, and other items. **Farriers** <term>mareſcalchi: craftsmen who shod horses and acted as early veterinarians.</term> do not overlook them either, as they are good for removing **spots** and **clouds** <note>cataracts or corneal scarring</note>, or other blemishes that occur in the eyes of horses. When mixed with **sugar candy** <note>refined, crystallized sugar</note> and a little **white vitriol** <term>vitriolo bianco: zinc sulfate, used historically in eye drops for its astringent and antiseptic properties.</term>, the whole being finely pulverized and blown into the afflicted eye, it heals it in a short time; and the same is good for men.

...that is to say, **wheat**, and other grains which they happen to possess; and so that these do not sprout from the moisture, they gnaw off the germ <note>The author refers to the ant's instinct to bite off the embryo of a seed to prevent it from germinating in the nest.</note> and thus preserve it. If the grain has taken on some dampness during the winter, when the sun shines, they carry it outside to dry so that it does not rot; they also do this if the grain they are carrying is green, drying it before storing it away. 

Among themselves, they maintain almost a form of **Republic** <term>Republica: used here to describe a highly organized social structure with shared labor and mutual respect, a common comparison for social insects in the Renaissance.</term>. The elders remain at rest and do not labor, and they are respected by all. If there is any among them who is sick, they carry her out into the air for a while so that she may be somewhat revived, and then they return her inside in the same manner. If any of them should arrive with a heavy burden, they immediately run to help her. If the journey they must make to the harvest site is long, they station themselves at intervals along the path, where one unburdens the other—one goes and the other comes—and in this way, they reasonably share the labor. When one of them has died, two ants take her and carry her out, accompanied by many others, appearing almost as if they are mourning the loss of their companion. 

In the end, it is admirable to consider the virtues of these little animals. Regarding **medicine**, they are not in common use, except in venereal medicines <note>original: "medicamenti antiueneri"; while the term often refers to cures for venereal disease, the text specifies its use as an aphrodisiac.</note>, for the **oil made from winged ants** is excellent for inciting the **appetite of Venus** <note>A poetic reference to sexual desire or libido.</note>. ### Concerning Spiders. Chapter 19.

There are many species of spiders, but here I do not intend to speak of any except the large ones, which are of various colors. Those who wish to see how many species and names they have should consult Mattioli <note>Pietro Andrea Mattioli (1501–1578), a renowned Italian physician and botanist.</note> on Dioscorides <note>Pedanius Dioscorides, the ancient Greek author of *De Materia Medica*, the foundational text for Western pharmacology.</note>, where they will be fully satisfied. Here, I only intend to speak of their virtues against fevers. Some claim that placing a live spider inside a hazelnut shell and hanging it around the neck cures quartan fever <term>febre quartana: a type of malaria characterized by a fever that recurs every third day.</term>; but Schröder <note>Johann Schröder (1600–1664), a German physician whose *Pharmacopoeia Medico-Chymica* was a standard reference in the 17th century.</note> in his *Medical-Chemical Pharmacopoeia*, provides a recipe for a fever-reducing plaster <term>empiastro febrifugo: a medicinal patch applied to the skin to combat fever.</term> which he assures is very effective, and I did not want to fail to translate that recipe.

## On Scorpions. Chapter 20.

Scorpions kill with their sting, and it is particularly most harmful to virgins <note>In early modern medical belief, young women were often thought to be more susceptible to certain poisons due to their supposedly "cold and moist" temperament.</note>; but with their own life, they remedy such damage, restoring health to those whom they intended to deprive of life with their venomous sting. For when they are themselves crushed and placed over the wound, they draw to themselves every bit of poison that could harm the patient, and thus they avert the danger.

But human ingenuity, in order to remove every inconvenience that might arise—both because of the difficulty of having a live scorpion immediately at hand, and also because many would abhor such an unsightly remedy—has found a way to make various oils from them. These are not only helpful for their venomous bite or sting, but also possess many other virtues, as we shall describe regarding some of them below...

Now, just as the Cat by natural antipathy <note>In early modern science, "antipathy" was a natural or "occult" repulsion between certain animals or substances that were considered instinctive enemies.</note> is the enemy of the Mouse, and reciprocally the Mouse of the Cat, the Weasel of the Serpent, the Lion of the Rooster, and so many other animals that are irreconcilable, living in continuous war; so the Scorpion is the mortal enemy of the Spider, for it continually seeks them out to serve as nourishment. 

Those who hunt Scorpions know this: they take some straws or stems and, bringing them close to the holes in old walls where they presume Scorpions to be, they imitate with these the movement of Spiders. The Scorpion, believing it to be a Spider, comes out to catch it and is captured by those men with some small pincers <note>Small tongs or forceps used for safe handling of venomous creatures.</note> that they carry for this purpose.

I do not want to omit recounting a curiosity told to me by a friend of mine worthy of faith, which he himself observed and saw of a Spider and a Scorpion, which is most curious. A very large Spider having woven a web on a wall, a Scorpion happened there by ill fortune, falling from the wall into it. Being entangled in said web (which, due to its great size, did not break), it could go neither forward nor backward. And the Spider, seeing its enemy imprisoned, did not want to let such a fine opportunity pass to avenge itself of an enemy that one day, without fail, could [harm it]...

He then resolved [to act] in the manner of the Rhinoceros <note>This refers to a popular early modern belief, originating in ancient texts like those of Pliny the Elder, that the rhinoceros was the elephant's natural mortal enemy and would specifically target the elephant's softer underbelly.</note>, which, when fighting the Elephant and being unable to wound him in any place other than the belly—since in all other places the skin is extremely hard—gets underneath him and wounds him with his very sharp horn, and thus kills and conquers him. He went back, went under his web, and began to wound the enemy in the belly, killing him with just a few blows. 

He circled and returned to the heights, and from a distance observed whether [the scorpion] was truly dead, or if he were merely faking. He drew closer, and yet still did not feel confident enough to approach entirely; he stopped, and observed anew. ## On Certain Oils of Scorpions.
### Chapter 21.

**Simple Oil of Scorpions**, which is ordinarily made with oil of **bitter almonds**, where fifty scorpions—collected at the proper time, as was stated in the nineteenth chapter—are infused in every pound of it and left for forty days in the sun; besides being good for their own stings, it is also excellent for **colic pains** when placed in <term>enemas</term> <note>original: "cristieri," referring to clysters or enemas used to deliver medication into the colon.</note>, it provokes urine, is helpful for <term>nephritic</term> <note>Relating to the kidneys.</note> pains, and expels **kidney stones**.

Similarly, the **compound of Mesue** <note>Johannes Mesue, a likely semi-legendary figure of Arabic medicine whose works were standard in European pharmacies.</note> is beneficial; in addition to helping with the aforementioned conditions, it heals the bite of any venomous animal, mitigates **earaches**, and by anointing the spine and the wrists during <term>paroxysms</term> <note>The sudden onset or intensification of symptoms, such as the chills or shakes of a fever.</note>, it helps against fevers, particularly **tertian** and **quartan** <note>Types of malaria-like fevers that recur every three or four days.</note>. Our own oil, which is made as we shall describe hereafter, does not yield in virtue to that of **Mattioli** <note>Pietro Andrea Mattioli (1501–1577), a famous Italian physician and botanist whose "Commentaries" on Dioscorides were the gold standard of the era.</note>; rather, it operates with more activity and has many other virtues, as will be described.

# OF BEES,
## and their parts.

### SIXTH QUARTER.

### Chapter 22.

We have reserved the discussion of Bees for the very end, as they are the creatures that produce honey, so that with its sweetness and flavor, it may temper the unpleasant tastelessness of my writing. Nevertheless, I know that the discernment of whoever reads these works of mine will recognize my good intentions, excusing me as a man if I have made any errors in some matter. Now, returning to our subject of Bees, I say that on their own, dried and crushed, they are beneficial to those whose hair is falling out, and they make the fallen hair grow back; this is done by mixing them with some suitable oil, such as Oil of Wax <note>A medicinal oil traditionally produced through the dry distillation of beeswax.</note>, or of Bitter Almonds, or of distilled Tartar <note>Distilled from the crusty deposits found in wine barrels (potassium bitartrate), it was highly valued in early modern chemistry and pharmacy for its supposed purifying properties.</note>, which is the most excellent of all, or other similar substances. The bee itself, crushed and applied directly onto its own sting, helps miraculously. Its constituent parts are honey, wax, and propolis <term>propulo</term> <note>Modern propolis; a resinous substance collected by bees from tree buds, used as a sealant and "glue" within the hive.</note>, which is that bitumen with which the bees seal the cracks of their vessels <note>The author uses "vessels" to refer to the structure of the beehive or the individual cells of the honeycomb.</note>, and I shall discuss each of these things separately.

# Of Honey. Chapter 23.

Honey is by its nature hot and dry in the second degree <note>In Galenic medicine, substances were classified by their "temperament" (hot, cold, moist, or dry) on a scale of one to four to determine how they would balance the body's humors.</note>, and possesses nutritious, cleansing <term>abstersive</term>, and opening <term>aperitive</term> <note>These terms refer to the substance's ability to clear blockages in the body's vessels or cleanse wounds and tissues.</note> virtues; it provokes urine, is suitable for the lungs, helps a cough, and resists putrefaction. When applied externally, it is excellent for "clouds" in the eyes <note>Likely referring to cataracts or corneal scarring.</note> and blurring of the vision. Many things are made from honey through the art of distillation, as we shall discuss; in places where there is a lack of wine, one can make vinous Hydromel <note>Commonly known as mead.</note>, which is a drink very similar in smell and taste to wine.

It is made by taking one part of honey and eight parts of spring water; for example <note>original: "verbi gratia"</note>, for every pound of honey, throw in an ounce of finely crushed crude Tartar <note>The potassium bitartrate crust found in wine barrels, used here as a fermenting agent.</note>. Place the water in a large cauldron, according to the quantity of the said Hydromel you wish to make, putting the aforementioned tartar inside so that it dissolves in the water, which must be brought to a boil. Then, the honey should be added and dissolved well together, and placed in a small barrel <term>caratello</term> or in an earthenware vessel, in a place where it is exposed to the sun, or lacking that, in a heated room <term>stufa</term>. Let it ferment there for thirty or forty days until it has acquired the smell and taste of wine; then, transfer it to another vessel, separating it from the dregs <term>brutezza</term>, and place it in a cellar or another cool place where wine is preserved.

The said Hydromel <note>mead</note> benefits those who suffer from urinary ailments, stones <note>kidney or bladder stones</note>, and similar conditions; one can also make from it an aqua vitae <note>literally "water of life," referring to a distilled spirit or brandy</note> similar to that made from wine, although in small quantity.

Vinegar is also made from honey, as follows.

Take one part of Honey and eight parts of common water; let it cook until it is reduced by half, and place it in an earthenware or wooden vessel in a warm place, as was mentioned above. Suspend within it a rag containing some crushed Mustard seed, and in a short time it will become acidic. The said vinegar can then be distilled to extract a distilled vinegar, which serves to dissolve any kind of precious stones without any prior calcination <note>The process of heating a substance to high temperatures to reduce it to a powder or change its chemical state; the author suggests this distilled honey vinegar is a powerful enough solvent to bypass this step.</note>, as shall be told, if it pleases God, in another book which I intend to bring to light if God gives me life.

### Quintessence of Honey. Chap. 25.

Take a good quantity of honey with the honeycombs, and place it in a glass vessel <note>original: *bozza*</note> in a bain-marie <term>bagno Maria</term> <note>A water bath used for gentle, indirect heating.</note>, drawing out all the water that may come forth; leave the rest in the boiling bath for four or five days, and then put the distilled water back on top to extract the tincture from it according to the art <note>A phrase referring to the established rules and procedures of alchemy.</note>. Once filtered, let it be digested <note>Subjected to gentle, steady heat to encourage chemical maturation.</note> and purified of all dross by filtering it again. Once this is done, let it be distilled in the [water] bath until dry, sealing the receiver very well so that it does not breathe <note>Meaning it must be airtight to prevent the escape of volatile vapors.</note>. The distillate is the element of Air, and what remains at the bottom is the element of Fire.

Then, from the dregs <note>original: *fecci*</note> remaining above, draw out the oil using a retort <term>storta</term> <note>A glass vessel with a long, downward-pointing neck used for distilling substances that require higher heat.</note>; the remainder being thoroughly calcined <note>Heated to high temperatures until reduced to ash.</note>, the salt is extracted from these dregs with common water. Once purified, we have [all elements] together: with the Air, the Water; and with the essence, the Oil; the Fire; and the Salt representing the Earth. Take, therefore, the aforementioned four elements, which, having been perfectly purged of all heterogeneity <note>Impurities or dissimilar substances.</note>, will form a new essential body, far more noble than that in which they were [originally contained].

### *Of Wax. Chap. 26.*

Wax is of a most balanced temperament, and for this reason it adapts to every quality. There is no ointment or plaster <term>cerotto</term> <note>A medical dressing made of wax, oil, or resin spread on cloth.</note> so hot or cold that wax does not usually enter into it, as it serves to give the mixture body without altering the medicinal virtue of the ingredients added to them.

An oil is made from it, well known through distillation, which is excellent for joint pains <note>original: *giōture*</note> and earaches, soothing and softening marvelously. It is of a subtle and penetrating nature, and there is no known instance where its application to a part of the body has caused harm to anyone, as often happens with some other medicines.

The said oil, taken internally, helps to provoke urine when four or five drops are given in a suitable liquid <note>A "vehicle" or carrier liquid such as wine, water, or broth.</note>. <meta>This page transitions from the end of the alphabetical index (found on the previous page) to the formal title page and introductory praise for the work of Carlo Lancillotti. # The Most Elaborate Chemical Work
# OF CARLO LANCILLOTTI,
## **Doctor of Medicine.**

->*EULOGY.*<-
<note>original: *ELOGIVM*; a formal speech or piece of writing that praises someone or something highly.</note>

> It sails again, but under better auspices:
->The New Argo.<-
<note>In Greek mythology, the *Argo* was the ship of Jason and the Argonauts. Here, the author compares his book to a vessel seeking the "Golden Fleece" of chemical knowledge.</note>
Not to seize gold, but to produce it.
->Since it was nothing else<-
That gold of the Argolic Ship—the Fleece—
(If only one may draw back the veil from the fables)
->Than a Chemical Book,<-
By which the secret dogmas of <term>Chrysopoeia</term>
<note>Chrysopoeia (from Greek *chrysos*, "gold," and *poiein*, "to make") is the alchemical term for the transmutation of base metals into gold.</note>
->Were made public.<-
Indeed, this Book also
->Teaches and creates treasures.<-
And that which under the vigilant protection of the Dragon,
In such a religious custody of darkness,
->Was once detained,<-
<note>This refers to the dragon that guarded the Golden Fleece in the grove of Ares. The author suggests that alchemical secrets were once "guarded" or hidden in darkness/obscurity but are now being revealed.</note>
Now is better than that, and of its own accord
Comes forth into the light for the public good of mortals.
Having read this, and having chosen it from thousands,
Fabulous Midas is no longer believed <note>i.e., the story of Midas is no longer seen as just a myth.</note>,
Since whatever is touched and seen in it
->Becomes plainly golden.<-
Oh! What a storehouse of Chemistry,
->Reader,<-
From which it is possible to draw out
Not only the Author’s ingenuity, but also a spirit
->To help you.<-

<vocab>Carlo Lancillotti, Alchemy, Chymica, Chrysopoeia, Argo, Midas, Vellus Aureum</vocab>

<keywords>Carlo Lancillotti, alchemy, Chrysopoeia, Golden Fleece, Argo, Midas, chemical treatise, 17th-century medicine</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the introductory eulogy (Elogium) for Carlo Lancillotti’s chemical work. It transitions from the mythological metaphors of the "New Argo" on the previous page to a more specific celebration of the alchemist’s power over the elements and planetary metals.</meta>

Truly, at how much must the Inventor of so great a Work be valued,
->who not only seasoned Chemical salts<-
->but even Venus herself into medicines.<-
<note>original: *Venerem*. In the language of alchemy, Venus refers to the metal **Copper**. The author is praising the chemist's ability to transform raw metals into healing preparations.</note>
Who with his command stabilized
->the restless Spirits of Mercury:<-
<note>Mercury (quicksilver) was famously difficult for early chemists to "fix" or stabilize because of its volatility; the author credits Lancillotti with mastering this "restless" element.</note>
Who by his own industry awakened
->the idle slowness of Saturn<-
<note>original: *Saturni*. Saturn refers to the metal **Lead**, traditionally associated with heaviness, dullness, and the "slow" pace of the outermost known planet.</note>
->What more can be said?<-
With him acting, and stirring up the flames,
all the Elements felt the power of the Chemical
->art.<-
Moreover, even Poisons themselves, through their most excellent
->Artisan,<-
->learned innocence:<-
<note>This refers to the iatrochemical practice—popularized by Paracelsus—of purifying toxic substances to harness their medicinal properties without their "venom."</note>
->And as if it had been too little<-
to educate for Medicine the metals
->condemned to the bowels of the Earth,<-
he also transferred the Planets themselves—but no longer
->wandering—<-
->from Heaven<-
->into Chemical uses.<-
<note>The word "Planet" is derived from the Greek word for "wanderer." The author suggests that by capturing planetary forces in chemical medicines, they are no longer "wandering" in the sky but are anchored for human benefit.</note>

<summary>This page concludes a celebratory eulogy for Carlo Lancillotti, praising his alchemical skill in transforming "restless" and "slow" planetary metals—specifically copper, mercury, and lead—into safe and effective medicinal remedies.</summary>

# Errors found in the printing, including only the most essential ones, as others are left to the correction of the discerning Reader.

## PART ONE.

Page 33. line 9. exhalation, read exaltation:
<note>original: *esalatione* / *esaltatione*. In alchemy, "exaltation" refers to a process that raises a substance to a higher purity or dignity.</note>

## PART THREE.

Page 16. line 12. *sendoni*, read *tendoni*.
<note>The word *tendoni* likely refers to "tendons" or perhaps large "awnings/coverings" depending on the specific chemical apparatus described on that page.</note>
Pag. 27. line 1: add *volte* <note>original: *volte*. This can mean "times" or "vaults."</note>.
Page ibid. line 23. *cola*, read *cooba*.
<note>original: *cooba*. This is a technical term for **cohobation**, an alchemical process where a distillate is poured back onto its residue and re-distilled to increase its potency.</note>
Page 28. line 15. *cola*, read *cooba*.
Page 36. line 9. ratifying, read rarefying.
<note>original: *ratificandosi* / *rarificandosi*. Rarefication refers to the process of making a substance less dense, often through heat.</note>
Page 41. line 11. senseless, read condensed:
<note>original: *insensato* / *condensato*.</note>
Page 52. line 28. *hypoplexy*, read apoplexy.
<note>original: *ipoplessia* / *apoplessia*. Apoplexy was a historical term for a stroke or sudden loss of consciousness.</note>
Page 35. and 36. where *ana manip. v.*, read *ana manip. fl.*, that is, half.
<note>original: *ana manip.* This is pharmaceutical shorthand. *Ana* means "of each" and *manip.* stands for *manipulus* or "handful." The correction clarifies the specific quantity to be used in a recipe.</note>
Page 57. line 31. sign, read kingdom.
<note>original: *segno* / *regno*. Likely referring to the "mineral kingdom" or "vegetable kingdom."</note>
Page 58. line 5. *Eliana*, read Aelianus.
<note>original: *Eliano*. Likely referring to Claudius Aelianus, a Roman author and teacher of rhetoric who wrote about natural history.</note>
Page 59. line 24. and in this they proceed, read which precede this.
Page 58. line 4. Dark Sea, read Tuscan Sea;
<note>original: *Mar fosco* / *Mar Tosco*.</note>
Ibid. line 22. *empunertica*, read *emporetica*.
<note>original: *emporetica*. From the Greek *emporetikos* (belonging to commerce); *Charta emporetica* was a grade of unsized paper used by apothecaries for filtering or wrapping medicines.</note>
Page 63. line 8. *astensivo*, read *astersivo*.
<note>original: *astersivo*. An "astersive" or "abstersive" is a cleansing or detergent substance used to wash away impurities or heal wounds.</note>
Page 72. at the end add: A piece of steel, and soaking linen cloths therein.

<meta>This page continues the "Errata Corrige" (list of corrections) from the previous page, specifically focusing on technical corrections for later sections of the work. It transitions from general typographical errors to specific alchemical and medical terminology that could alter the meaning of the recipes or procedures if left uncorrected.</meta>

Page 82. line 18. and saline, read and saline.
<note>original: *e salina* / *e salina*. The OCR suggests identical words; this may have corrected a subtle punctuation error, a lowercase/uppercase distinction, or a typeface issue not captured in the transcription.</note>

Page 85. line 30: cohobating, read corroborating.
<note>original: *coobando* / *coroborando*. <term>Cohobation</term> is the alchemical process of pouring a distillate back onto its residue. To "corroborate" a medicine meant to strengthen its physiological effects.</note>

Page 92. line 5. dislations, read dislocations.
<note>original: *dislationi* / *dislocationi*. This refers to the medical correction of joints that have moved out of place.</note>

Page 105. line 30. Nibio, read There.
<note>original: *Nibio* / *Ibi*. "Nibio" refers to a kite (a type of bird), while the Latin *Ibi* means "in that place," typically used in citations to refer to a previously mentioned source.</note>

Page 109. line 3. pact, read passage.
<note>original: *patto* / *passo*. In this context, "passage" likely refers to a specific movement or a section of the text.</note>

Page 116. line 16. of salt, read of spirit of salt.
<note>original: *del sale* / *del spirito di sale*. <term>Spirit of salt</term> is the historical name for hydrochloric acid, a much more potent substance than common table salt.</note>

Page 146. line 30. Marcino, read Marine.
<note>original: *Marcino* / *Marino*. "Marino" refers to substances derived from the sea, such as sea salt or seaweed.</note>
